title: Ultrafast dynamics of vibronically dressed core excitons in graphite: a femtosecond RIXS perspective

paper_content.abstract: Time-resolved resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (tr-RIXS) is a powerful technique for probing quasiparticle interactions in quantum materials under nonequilibrium conditions. Here, we implement tr-RIXS at the carbon K-edge to investigate the ultrafast dynamics of core excitons coupled to vibrational modes in graphite. Using femtosecond X-ray pulses from a free-electron laser, we monitor the temporal evolution of vibronically dressed excitons and their interaction with symmetry-selective optical phonons. By tuning the incident photon energy across the 1s → σ* resonance and analyzing the integrated inelastic sideband intensity, we reveal a detuning-controlled crossover between two complementary dynamical regimes. Phenomenological modeling and first-principles calculations reproduce both the magnitude and detuning dependence of the spectral-weight changes. In this work, enabled by the unique capabilities of X-ray free-electron lasers, we demonstrate how tr-RIXS can access coupled electronic and lattice dynamics with elemental and symmetry specificity, opening new routes to control vibronic interactions in light-element and low-dimensional quantum materials.
paper_content.introduction:
Excitons, defined as Coulomb-bound electron-hole pairs, play a fundamental role in understanding various phenomena in condensed matter physics. These states emerge across a wide range of materials, including semiconductors, molecules, semimetals, low-dimensional systems, and metals with weak electronic screening1. Among excitonic subclasses, core excitons (CE) remain relatively unexplored. These excitons form when a photon excites an electron from a core atomic level into the conduction band, resulting in a strongly localized Frenkel excitonic state2. Despite their typically short lifetimes (≤10 fs, depending on the core level and atomic species), CEs significantly impact the scattering processes in material where exciton screening is ineffective.

A key manifestation of CE effects is the renormalization of X-ray absorption spectra (XAS). At the carbon K-edge, XAS provides critical insights into the electronic properties of molecules and graphitic systems2–11. However, the spectra are shaped by intermediate excitonic states, necessitating advanced theoretical modeling for accurate interpretation. Furthermore, CEs significantly influence the structure of resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) spectra. Recent research demonstrates that CEs can activate optical phonons8,12–16, emphasizing the dynamic coupling between excitons and phonons. This coupling is particularly critical in time-resolved RIXS, where photoinduced screening of CEs and the excitation of strongly coupled hot optical phonons alter the spectroscopic fingerprints of exciton-phonon interactions.

The electronic screening of core holes, a complex and pivotal aspect of light-matter interactions, determines the spectral features in both XAS and RIXS. Although metals efficiently screen core holes because of their high density of conduction electrons, leading to negligible excitonic effects, materials with reduced screening capabilities can sustain bound excitonic states. CEs may distort the local crystal lattice in such systems, resulting in vibronically dressed excitons that enhance phonon activation.

Graphite, a two-dimensional material with pronounced electronic anisotropy, provides an exemplary case for studying CE-phonon interactions2,5,8,17. Experimental and theoretical investigations have shown that carbon 1s core holes in graphite, which are inadequately screened in this van der Waals system, trigger multiple scatterings of CEs with optical phonons. These phonons are activated by local Jahn-Teller (JT) distortions caused by the unscreened core hole.

In this study, our objective was to modulate the screening efficiency of core holes in graphite, induced by femtosecond extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses, and to monitor the temporal evolution of the vibronic dressing of CEs. By optically exciting the system to generate hot electrons in the conduction band, we increased the available charge density in this semimetal, enhancing the screening capability. The extent of screening was indirectly probed through the dynamics of the phonon sidebands in the RIXS loss spectrum, serving as a qualitative indicator of exciton-phonon coupling strength (ExPC). Throughout this work, the coupling between lattice vibrations and the core-excited state is referred to as exciton-phonon coupling, rather than the more general term electron-phonon coupling. This distinction is important, as the resonant inelastic signal in RIXS originates from interactions between phonons and the localized charge distribution associated with the core-exciton intermediate state. While early RIXS studies often described such coupling in terms of electron-phonon interactions, recent literature (e.g., 13) has clarified that, under strong resonance conditions, the extracted coupling constants should be more accurately interpreted as exciton-phonon in nature.

Only a handful of tr-RIXS studies have been reported to date, primarily targeting electronic and magnetic excitations in transition-metal compounds such as cuprates, iridates, and vanadates18–24. These pioneering works have demonstrated the potential of Free Electron Laser (FEL)-based tr-RIXS to resolve transient phenomena such as ultrafast melting and recovery of magnetic order, the interplay between spin and lattice degrees of freedom, and light-induced changes in orbital and charge correlations. Theoretical and computational advances have further highlighted the sensitivity of RIXS to coupled electron-lattice dynamics25,26. However, direct time-domain access to phonon excitations—particularly in light-element systems—has remained beyond reach due to technical challenges in both energy resolution and spectral interpretation.

To our knowledge, this is the first time-resolved RIXS study to report a pump-induced reduction of ExPC at the carbon 1s → σ* resonance in graphite, approximately 8 eV above the Fermi level, where the intermediate state lies in the σ conduction manifold. Previous ultrafast studies in graphitic systems have primarily focused on near-EF excitations, revealing that the electron-phonon coupling (EPC) strength can either increase or decrease depending on the excitation conditions, such as in coherent-phonon generation or electronic softening mechanisms27,28. More recently, time-resolved experiments and first-principles simulations in transition-metal dichalcogenides have demonstrated that EPC itself can be renormalized in nonequilibrium conditions, with modifications in phonon lifetimes, band dispersions, and mode-specific coupling matrix elements under optical pumping29,30. However, those studies were limited to low-energy Dirac-like bands and did not probe the deeper-lying σ* states relevant for core-level RIXS. These works collectively underscore that EPC is a dynamic quantity, not a fixed material parameter, and its evolution can serve as a sensitive probe of many-body interactions under ultrafast excitation. Our findings extend this perspective, revealing how photoexcited π − π* carriers transiently suppress ExPC via enhanced screening in the σ* manifold.

By studying the dynamics of ExPC at the carbon K-edge in graphite, we capture the femtosecond evolution of vibronically dressed CE following ultrafast photoexcitation and establish a new spectroscopic window into phonon-coupled excitonic states and extend the reach of tr-RIXS into the domain of weakly screened systems.
paper_content.results:
Pump-probe RIXS scheme and experimental layout
A conceptual scheme of the RIXS process in graphite is depicted in Fig. 1a, b. An incident X-ray photon promotes an electron from the 1s core orbital in the ground state to the 2sp2 σ bands, where it experiences a partially screened potential caused by the core hole. The presence of the core hole in the intermediate state induces a substantial modification in the local atomic configuration around the interaction site5,12,16,31–34. This modification arises from the ionic coupling between the core exciton and lattice phonon systems, leading to dynamical symmetry breaking within the core-excited states. As a result, a significant JT distortion (~0.20 Å)8,35 occurs, displacing the core-excited atom from its equilibrium position in the ground state.

The excited electron subsequently relaxes in a few femtoseconds (the inverse of the natural linewidth Γ associated with the core-hole state) to fill the core hole, emitting a photon in the process. The energy difference between the incident and scattered photons manifests as overtones corresponding to the energy of the phonons ℏωp remaining in the final state as depicted in Fig. 1b.

Representative static RIXS loss spectra measured in this experiment are shown in Fig. 1c. The black and gray curves correspond to on-resonance and off-resonance conditions, respectively, and were acquired with an experimental energy resolution of approximately 350 meV. For comparison, a high-resolution RIXS loss spectrum from Feng et al.12, measured at a similar incident photon energy with a resolution of ~50 meV, is also included. This comparison highlights the presence of a broad loss tail in our on-resonance spectrum, consistent with previously reported vibronic progressions despite the lower resolution.

The high-resolution carbon K-edge RIXS spectrum of graphite exhibits a prominent elastic peak at 0 eV energy loss, accompanied by a sequence of equally spaced inelastic features attributed to vibronic replicas arising from ExPC12,14,36. These overtones correspond primarily to the coupling between CE and the zone-center E2g phonon mode, with an energy of approximately 196 meV, and follow a characteristic Poissonian progression as described by the Ament model31. Each overtone reflects an increasing number of phonon excitations, representing a quantized vibrational ladder coupled to the intermediate core-exciton state37. Recent work by Dashwood et al.14 demonstrated that a complete interpretation of this fine structure requires a full multi-mode analysis, as the phonon sidebands include contributions not only from the E2g mode at Γ but also from finite-momentum phonons such as the A0 mode at K, which produce asymmetric lineshapes and mixed-mode replicas. In particular, the detuning dependence of the multiphonon envelope was shown to be sensitive to both the phonon dispersion and the momentum-dependent EPC matrix elements.

In the present experiment, individual vibronic overtones are not resolved due to the limited energy resolution (see spectra in Fig. 1c). However, a broad inelastic sideband is clearly visible in the resonant on- and off-resonance spectra and represents the loss tail. Reprinted with permission from X. Feng et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 116401 (2020). Copyright (2020) American Physical Society. d Schematic representation of the RIXS excitation scheme and photoinduced processes. The green solid arrow indicates the optical pump pulse, tuned to the resonant energy corresponding to the π → π* transition at the M saddle point of the Brillouin zone (BZ). This process generates photoexcited hot electrons that are primarily confined between the graphene layers. Due to the peculiar band topology of graphite, the resulting bottleneck in the phonon channel deexcitation prolongs the average lifetime of valence-band quasiparticles27,41,78. The blue dashed arrow represents the X-ray probe absorption process, promoting a 1s core-level electron into the σ* conduction band at the Γ point. The intermediate state persists for an effective scattering duration τs, which depends on both the intrinsic core-hole lifetime and the photon energy detuning36,79.

Static and pumped RIXS across the CK σ-edge in graphite
The X-ray absorption spectrum of graphite is shown in Fig. 2a at both the π and σ thresholds. The peak at the lower photon energy (~284 eV) corresponds to the transition of the 1s photoelectron into the unoccupied out-of-plane 2pπ* orbitals (1s → π*). Conversely, the peak at a higher energy (~291.8 eV) is assigned to contributions from the hybridized 2sp2 σ in-plane σ* (C-C) orbitals. This higher energy edge does not directly reflect the electronic dynamics induced by the photoexcitation of the π → π* transition. Instead, it primarily responds to structural changes within the material’s configuration50. The graphite XAS is predominantly influenced by Frenkel-type excitonic effects at resonance energies. The Frenkel-like exciton is primarily localized on the core-excited site with appreciable weight on nearest neighbors (spatial extent of a few bonds), rather than a fully delocalized Wannier state2,4,11,53.

The one-electron density of states alone does not explain the absorption spectra because the excited electron occupies a highly localized state pulled off the bottom of the band gap. This mechanism leads to the appearance of white lines and a significant modification of the XAS cross-section54. Similar effects are evident in the resonant emission spectra of graphite at the carbon K edge7,8,55–58.

In Fig. 2b, c, the experimental data illustrate the impact of core-exciton vibronic interactions on the loss spectra in both the ground and the optically excited states. Figure 2b shows the unpumped loss spectra of graphite (black curves), recorded at FEL photon energies (indicated by coloured markers in panel a) tuned across the K σ resonance. These spectra are plotted as a function of energy loss and displayed in order of increasing photon energies. The on-resonance spectra are compared with an off-resonance unpumped spectrum (blue curve), recorded at a photon energy beyond the absorption edge (blue open circle in Fig. 2a). As aforementioned, when the photon energy hν is tuned close to the absorption resonance (hνres ~291.8 eV), thereby reducing the energy detuning value Ω = h(ν − νres), an asymmetric incoherent loss shoulder emerges, as indicated by the coloured areas between the blue and black curves in Fig. 2b. Figure 2c displays the corresponding pumped loss spectra (red solid lines), acquired at a fixed pump-probe delay of 150 fs. These are compared against two references: (i) the unpumped spectra recorded at the same photon energies (black dashed lines), and (ii) the off-resonance spectrum (blue curve), whose intensity is rescaled as discussed below.

The lineshape of the off-resonance spectrum lacks the asymmetric loss tail and exhibits a symmetric profile. This symmetry arises because, in the emission process, the final state of the RIXS process mirrors the initial state and does not involve ExPC scattering (see Supplementary Note 7 in SI for further discussion). This portion of the spectrum is commonly referred to as the coherent component. We note that the apparent increase in spectral intensity at energy losses below −2.5 eV in the off-resonant spectrum shown in SI is not due to an asymmetry of the elastic or inelastic phonon features, but rather reflects the onset of valence band emission, as shown in the full-range spectrum provided in the SI Supplementary Note 2, Fig. 2.

Particular attention should be given to the pair of pumped and unpumped spectra measured off-resonance (top spectra in panel c of Fig. 2, blue open dot), specifically at a photon energy of 294.5 eV with a detuning of approximately Ω = 2.7 eV. In this case, the overtone tails are absent due to the large detuning value, and the spectra are symmetric. Furthermore, the effect of the pump on the excited spectrum is negligible, as indicated by the complete overlap of the pumped and unpumped spectra. This lack of pump-induced changes in the off-resonance spectra is a key observation, highlighting that the influence of the photoinduced electron-hole pairs predominantly impacts the excitonic state and its dynamics. Properties such as exciton energy, screening, and vibronic coupling are affected, while the density of states remains largely unchanged in the out-of-equilibrium state.

In this work, the limited energy resolution (~350 meV) of the RIXS spectra prevents a clean spectral separation between the elastic peak and low-energy phonon sidebands. As a result, direct access to the absolute inelastic intensity is not feasible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a relative metric R(Ω) that tracks the integrated excess weight in the loss region as a function of photon energy detuning Ω. Importantly, R(Ω) is not a direct measurement of the absolute phonon spectral weight, but rather a baseline-independent proxy that captures its detuning- and pump-dependent modulation. To ensure that this proxy is robust and not sensitive to arbitrary assumptions about the elastic baseline or absorption cross-section, we implemented three independent normalization schemes: (i) a zero-loss alignment of the off-resonance spectrum as elastic reference, (ii) a normalization of the resonant spectra to the XAS absorption threshold at the corresponding photon energy, and (iii) an XAS-weighted scaling of the reference spectrum before subtraction. These approaches are described in detail in Supplementary Note 5 in SI, Fig. 6). All three methods yield a consistent trend for R(Ω), demonstrating that our conclusions do not rely on a specific treatment of the elastic baseline or absorption cross section. Because no method allows for a complete deconvolution of elastic and inelastic components at this resolution, we do not attempt to extract absolute ExPC constants from R(Ω). Instead, we focus on relative changes in R(Ω) between the pumped and unpumped conditions. These changes are interpreted as qualitative signatures of ExPC modulation in the non-equilibrium regime.

For the pump-probe data, we applied the same zero-loss rescaling procedure using the off-resonant reference spectrum, ensuring full consistency with the unpumped analysis. This choice allows direct comparison between equilibrium and photoexcited conditions within the same normalization framework, without introducing additional assumptions about absorption or elastic-inelastic separation.

Detuning Ω controls inelastic weight and scattering time
The experimental inelastic proxy R(Ω), shown for both pumped Rp(Ω) (red colored stars) and unpumped Rup(Ω) (black colored stars) data in Fig. 3a, displays a clear resonant enhancement near the 1s → σ* absorption threshold and a monotonic decay at larger detuning. The detuning dependence of R(Ω) is qualitatively reproduced by integrated inelastic intensities computed from static Ament models incorporating one and two phonon modes. The resulting theoretical curves are shown in Fig. 3a as dashed blue (one-phonon) and red (two-phonon) lines, and compared to the experimental unpumped R(Ω). These two model variants yield nearly identical detuning trends after convolution with the experimental resolution, highlighting the robustness of R(Ω) as a resolution-limited indicator of total vibronic strength, and its insensitivity to the specific phonon composition assumed. The underlying RIXS spectra generated from these models are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 and Fig. 5, while the phonon coupling strengths M, Huang-Rhys factors g, and mode energies ω are listed in Supplementary Table 2. These parameters are extracted from high-resolution CK-edge studies by Feng12 and Dashwood14. Specifically, the two phonon modes used, ω1 = 0.196 eV and ω2 = 0.165 eV, correspond to the dominant E2g mode and a secondary lower energy mode, respectively. The associated couplings (M1 = 0.42 eV, M2 = 0.30 eV) and Huang-Rhys parameters (g1 = 4.59, g2 = 3.31) were chosen to reflect the strength and spacing of vibronic sidebands reported in those works. Additional details on the modeling assumptions, numerical implementation, and convolution procedure are provided in SI Supplementary Note 3, Figs. 3 and 4. This modeling is motivated by two considerations. First, under the moderate experimental energy resolution (~350 meV), individual phonon overtones are not resolved, and only the integrated inelastic weight in the [−2.5, 0] eV range can be reliably tracked.

Second, first-principles calculations of the electron-phonon coupling (see Fig. 3 panel c, and SI Supplementary Note 6, Fig. 7) show that the dominant coupling at the accessed energies involves zone-center optical phonons near the Γ point in the σ* conduction manifold. This result reflects the strong renormalization of the unoccupied σ* states by lattice vibrations, most prominently visible at k ≃ Γ, where the parabolic conduction band exhibits the largest spectral deformation compared to the equilibrium DFT band (white dashed line). This deformation arises from electron-phonon interactions and points to a dominant coupling to Γ-point optical phonons, in particular the E2g mode. Physically, when resonantly probing the C 1s → σ* transition, the excited electron occupies high-lying states in the σ* manifold several eV above EF, forming a bound core exciton with the localized 1s hole. At these excitation energies (~8 eV above EF), the electron resides near k=Γ, where the available phase space for scattering strongly favors small-q phonon modes. The electron-phonon phase space is constrained by momentum conservation, so the large density of states and the small-q nature of the transition point to the prevalence of Γ-point optical phonons as the dominant scattering channel. While the σ* band extends toward the M point - where van Hove singularities and finite-q phonons (e.g., at K or M) might contribute - our ab initio results show that the electron-phonon matrix elements and corresponding spectral renormalization are significantly weaker at those k-points. Therefore, Γ-point E2g phonons are expected to dominate the vibronic structure in the accessible intermediate-state manifold. This picture is further reinforced by prior theoretical work on the energy-dependent evolution of electron-phonon coupling channels in graphite and graphene. In particular, calculations by Margine and Giustino59 and Mazzola et al.60 demonstrate that the dominant phonon coupling mode depends strongly on the excitation energy. Near the Dirac point, coupling to the A0 phonon mode at the K point dominates, whereas at higher excitation energies associated with σ-like bands, the coupling shifts toward Γ-point optical phonons (E2g) and out-of-plane ZO modes. Extrapolating this trend to the higher-energy σ* resonance above EF indicates that small-q phonons are the most efficient scattering channels, consistent with the strong Γ-localized renormalization seen in our spectral-function calculations. Taken together, these results provide a solid microscopic foundation for employing an effective Einstein-mode description to capture the detuning dependence of the integrated inelastic spectral weight. They also justify the use of a single dominant mode in the phenomenological Ament-model envelope and reinforce the interpretation that the observed inelastic response arises primarily from coupling to zone-center optical phonons, without invoking phonon-mode resolution or fine-structure reproduction.

To contextualize this detuning behavior, Fig. 3b schematically illustrates the detuning dependence of the effective scattering time τs(Ω)-the characteristic duration during which the intermediate core-excited state remains active and can exchange energy with other degrees of freedom (see Supplementary Note 7 in SI, Fig. 8). This duration determines the temporal window over which phonon interactions can imprint signatures onto the RIXS final state. Near resonance (|Ω| ≪ Γ), τs is long and approximates 1/Γ, allowing sufficient time for vibronic dressing of the core exciton and strong coupling to optical phonons. In contrast, far off-resonance (|Ω| ≫ Γ), τs ~ 1/|Ω| becomes too short for coherent phonon processes to develop, and the inelastic intensity is suppressed. The crossover between these regimes follows τs(Ω) = 1/sqrt(Ω2 + Γ2), as introduced by Gel’mukhanov and co-workers36,61 and further discussed in15,31. This framework highlights how tr-RIXS acts as a temporal filter, selectively probing excitations based on their intrinsic timescales.

Upon optical excitation (pump-probe delay ~150 fs), the integrated inelastic weight Rp(Ω) is significantly reduced compared to the unpumped case Rup(Ω), consistent with transient screening of the core exciton and a weakening of ExPC. The contrast between pumped and unpumped spectra decreases progressively with detuning and vanishes far from resonance. This behavior reflects the detuning-dependent sensitivity of the RIXS cross section: near resonance, the intermediate core-excited state is strongly formed, allowing efficient coupling to lattice vibrations, whereas off-resonance the intermediate state becomes rapidly virtual and the interaction time (τs) too short for vibronic processes to develop. Consequently, the diminishing difference between R and Rp originates from reduced exciton-phonon interaction sensitivity at large |Ω|, rather than from changes in pump efficiency or overall screening strength. Since R integrates all unresolved phonon contributions, its suppression upon photoexcitation provides a clear qualitative signature of reduced ExPC in the σ* manifold under nonequilibrium conditions.

The effects of the optical pump on the parameters R (representing the inelastic component of the spectra) and r (the rescaling factor representing the coherent component, see caption of Fig. 2) suggest the following scenario. At a fixed delay of 150 fs between the pump and probe pulses, the coherent component r decreases compared to the unpumped case. Since r reflects changes in the absorption cross-section, its reduction indicates a decrease in the white line intensity characteristic of the resonant K-edge XAS spectrum. As the white line directly results from Frenkel core-exciton formation, this reduction provides initial evidence of core-exciton screening.

Interestingly, the similar detuning dependence of both R and r suggests that core-hole screening by the hot electrons and energy transfer from the electrons to the phononic system occur simultaneously. Johannsen et al.45 have shown that ultrafast electron dynamics in graphene, and similarly in graphite, involve rapid electron-electron scattering and thermalization of the electronic subsystem. This aligns with studies reporting sub-picosecond energy transfer to strongly coupled optical phonons, followed by energy dissipation through optical phonon emission46,62. These timescales agree well with the evolution of the phonon sideband spectral weight observed in the present study.

Detuning-dependent ultrafast dynamics
The temporal evolutions of the relative change ΔR(Ω, t)/R0(Ω) are plotted in the main panel of Fig. 4. Here, R(Ω, t) is the integrated inelastic RIXS weight (phonon-sideband proxy), and we plot ΔR/R ≡ [R(Ω, t) − R0(Ω)]/R0(Ω), where R0(Ω) is taken from the unpumped (negative-delay) spectrum. These dynamics were recorded at four different FEL photon energies across the resonance threshold, as indicated by the arrows in the inset of Fig. 4a. The analysis of the dynamic traces was carried out using a model double exponential decay-recovery function, as outlined in Supplementary Note 8 in SI, with a rapid decay time followed by a slower recovery process. The values corresponding to these ultrafast dynamic processes are plotted (black open circles) in the inset of Fig. 4a. The time traces reveal two distinct regimes as a function of the energy detuning Ω governed by different physical mechanisms. Rather than a sharp boundary, the time traces display a smooth crossover, whereby the relative weights of two mechanisms evolve continuously as Ω approaches the resonance threshold or moves away from it. As a result, the two regimes coexist, with their relative contributions to the ΔR/R dynamics varying continuously with Ω.

For small detuning (near threshold), the effective intermediate-state time is τs ≈ 10 fs (see also Supplementary Note 7 in SI, Fig. 8), and the inelastic sideband weight decays rapidly with a ~65 fs time constant, close to our resolution (Fig. 4a). This fast component reflects ultrafast screening of the core exciton by photoexcited carriers, which reduces exciton-phonon interactions and suppresses the local Jahn-Teller distortion; the corresponding microscopic picture is schematized in Fig. 4b by a transient displacement of a single carbon atom from equilibrium. The selectivity of this near-edge response, dominated by symmetry/orbital-resolved core-exciton intermediates at the Kσ edge, is consistent with attosecond K-edge measurements that resolve near-edge carrier dynamics on tens of femtoseconds and with theoretical descriptions of excitonic/vibronic near-edge behavior50.

As the detuning increases from the absorption threshold, τs drops below a few femtoseconds, suppressing the efficacy of coherent local lattice distortions. In this off-resonant window, the dynamics slow to a robust relaxation time of τ ~330 fs (Fig. 4a), which we assign to a nonthermal screening regime governed by two concurrent processes: energy-dependent quenching of the Jahn-Teller ExPC and the buildup of hot phonons via impulsive electron-phonon scattering. The evolution of this behavior with detuning is naturally explained by a growing scattering phase space: as the excitation energy moves toward the high-DOS σ* manifold, both electron-electron and electron-phonon scattering rates increase, enhancing quasiparticle decay and energy transfer to lattice vibrations. This picture is supported by GW-based lifetime calculations in graphite41, which show markedly reduced carrier lifetimes near van Hove singularities (e.g., π* saddle at M), and by attosecond K-edge XANES50, which identifies distinct relaxation pathways for π*- and σ*-derived states and links the σ* response to strong coupling with optical phonons on few-hundred-fs scales. The schematic in Fig. 4c depicts this off-resonant regime as the buildup and relaxation of collective hot phonon oscillations (SCOPs). While fundamentally different from near-Fermi-level dynamics, our observations are consistent with the broader hierarchy of relaxation timescales in graphitic systems. Specifically, (a) electron-electron thermalization near the Fermi level occurs within 10–100 fs, as measured by trARPES and THz spectroscopy63–65; (b) the sub-ps evolution of SCOP populations via strong mode-projected electron-phonon coupling is well documented in pump-probe and ultrafast optical studies62,65; and (c) full lattice thermalization and macroscopic strain effects develop only at multi-ps delays66–68. The off-resonant ~330 fs response observed here occupies a distinct window between ultrafast screening and long-timescale lattice expansion, governed by energy-resolved phonon dynamics. Finally, we stress that unlike low-energy probes such as trARPES and UED, which primarily access Dirac-like carriers near EF, tr-RIXS selectively addresses symmetry- and orbital-resolved excitonic states at the C K-edge, accessing a unique sector of the scattering phase space that governs nonthermal coupling pathways and hot-phonon behavior in the σ* regime.

To summarize, detuning acts as a selective control knob for complementary dynamical channels in graphite. Near the absorption threshold, tr-RIXS accesses symmetry- and orbital-resolved core-exciton intermediates at the Kσ edge, revealing a tens-of-femtoseconds suppression of the Jahn-Teller distortion driven by ultrafast exciton screening. As the detuning moves away from threshold, the evolving scattering phase space shortens electronic lifetimes and shifts the response into a nonthermal hot-phonon regime, where SCOPs are impulsively populated and relax on a few-hundred-femtosecond timescale41,50,62,65,69. This off-resonant regime corresponds to excitation energies approaching the σ* density of states, approximately 8 eV above the Fermi level, where the enhanced electronic screening originating from π → π* transitions (and the concomitant rise in carrier and phonon temperatures) leads to a marked reduction of the effective ExPC. The experiment therefore provides, for the first time, a direct observation, albeit qualitative, of the ultrafast modification of the ExPC constant g2 at high excitation energies, a parameter that is commonly assumed to remain fixed in time-resolved studies. These findings demonstrate that photoexcitation can dynamically tune the coupling strength between electronic and lattice degrees of freedom, providing a new handle on nonequilibrium screening phenomena in light-element materials. Subsequent anharmonic redistribution of the hot-phonon energy to acoustic modes46,52 and, at later times, full lattice thermalization and strain on multi-ps scales66–68 complete the energy-flow pathway. Overall, tr-RIXS reveals a previously unexplored regime in which the ExPC itself becomes transiently modified by the evolving screening environment, opening new possibilities for manipulating vibronic interactions at the core level.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation
Time-resolved RIXS experiments were performed on a highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) sample. Immediately before insertion into the UHV chamber of the MagneDyn endstation, the sample surface was freshly peeled in air to remove the topmost contaminated layers and expose a clean basal plane. The sample was then mounted with the graphite ab planes approximately perpendicular to the surface normal, such that the scattering geometry maximized sensitivity to in-plane σ states at the CK σ threshold.

Tr-RIXS measurements
The experiment was carried out at the time-resolved RIXS endstation of the MagneDyn beamline at the FERMI FEL (Elettra Sincrotrone Trieste, Italy)38. A standard pump–probe configuration, as described in ref. 38 was employed to probe the ultrafast dynamics of CE in graphite. For the probe, an extreme-ultraviolet/free-electron laser (FEL) pulse was tuned across the carbon K edge, resonant with the 1s!2sp2 σ transition (the Kσ threshold). The FEL polarization was maintained in the horizontal scattering plane, providing a substantial in-plane electric-field component and thereby enhancing the cross-section for excitations into the σ-bonding orbitals in the ab plane. The FEL beam impinged on the sample at an incidence angle of 30∘ with respect to the surface normal, quasi-collinear to the optical pump beam. Under these conditions, the scattering geometry (30∘ incidence and ~90∘ detection) corresponded to a small momentum transfer |q| ≈ 0.26 Å−1, close to the Brillouin-zone center, where zone-center optical phonons are preferentially probed. The incident FEL bandwidth, and hence the source energy resolution, was approximately 60 meV (see Supplementary Note 1 in the Supplementary Information). Inelastic RIXS spectra were recorded with a Scienta XES355 soft X-ray spectrometer70. Representative static loss spectra, acquired with this configuration, exhibited an overall experimental energy resolution of ~350 meV, obtained from the width of the elastic peak and dominated by the spectrometer response. The resonantly emitted photons were detected on a two-dimensional detector on a stroboscopic, pulse-to-pulse basis, enabling single-shot acquisition of spectra at each pump–probe delay. Details of the absolute energy calibration and determination of the instrumental energy resolution are provided in Supplementary Note 1 in the Supplementary Information. The sample was photoexcited by the third harmonic of the FERMI User laser, generated from the fundamental at 795 nm. The resulting ultraviolet pump pulses had a wavelength of 265 nm (photon energy 4.71 eV), p polarization, and operated at a repetition rate of 50 Hz38,71,72. Each pump pulse carried an energy of approximately 10 μJ at the sample. Taking into account the measured pump spot size and an incidence angle of 32.5∘ with respect to the surface normal, the optical fluence at the sample surface was about 32 mJ/cm2, corresponding to an estimated excitation of ~14% of the carbon atoms, as detailed in Supplementary Note 10 in the Supplementary Information. The pump photon energy was chosen to resonantly drive the π → π* transition at the M saddle point in the graphite Brillouin zone, thereby exciting valence quasiparticles in the 2p orbitals while keeping them decoupled from the σz states directly probed by the 1s!2sp2 σ core transition. This configuration mitigates saturation of the absorption channel and avoids pump-induced distortions of the x-ray absorption lineshape. The temporal overlap between pump and probe was established using a standard optical cross-correlation procedure at the beamline38, yielding an overall time resolution of approximately 50 fs (FWHM), limited by the convolution of the FEL and optical pulse durations and the timing-jitter compensation scheme. In this regime, the lifetime of the optically excited quasiparticles at the M point exceeds the experimental time resolution and significantly surpasses the typical C 1s core-exciton lifetime (~10 fs), ensuring that the tr-RIXS response is governed by the evolution of a long-lived valence-carrier population rather than by the core-hole decay alone. For additional background on the graphite C 1s absorption edges and excitonic response, we refer to Ahuja et al.2.

Theory
Ground state electronic band structure was calculated with Quantum Espresso (QE) plane-wave code with the use of semi-local PBE exchange-correlation functional73. Phonon dynamics and electron-phonon coupling calculations were performed with density functional perturbation theory74, where we combined QE-PHonon and EPW codes75. The latter code uses Wannier interpolation76 to provide phonon energies and electron-phonon matrix elements on a denser momentum grid, which are then needed to simulate Fan-Migdal electron self-energy and electron spectral function77. More details can be found in Supplementary Note 6 in the Supplementary Information.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Malvesuto et. al., look at the effect of pumping graphite on the (low resolution) RIXS specrtum following
pumping. The work is particularly timely, as LCLS-II is just turning on now which should increase the importance of time
resolved RIXS significantly. The RIXS spectrum as a function of detuning energy and being pumped is measured. The
spectrum is then broken down (to over simplify) by what part is due to electron phonon coupling and what part isn't. They use
this to determine information about graphite and its excited states.
While the results are well supported, and the methods appear to be sound, there are several issues I would like to see
resolved. In particular, the presentation does not make it easy for the reader to follow. Figure 2 is challenging to follow along.
The presentation of this figure is not optimal, and the authors should strongly consider splitting this figure into two figures. In
particular, figure d is challenging to understand, as the caption isn't particularly adequate, and one has to dig through the text
and the caption to really understand what is going on here. Relatedly, while I'm not sure figure 2S should be in the main text,
and in a sense the authors commitment to brevity is laudable, it makes it harder to follow as one has to read the SI and return
to really understand what is being presented. Incorporating some of that figure 3 might (or might not) help with clarity.
Basically, while I quite like the manuscript, I spent a noticable portion of time trying to figure out what was being presented.
In terms of science, a large portion of the results is pinned on the fitting of equation 1, which has 3 free parameters (although,
the justification for using this equation is well supported and justified). The changes between the ground and excited state
are quite large, but it is completely opaque to the reader how sensitive these fitting values are. Given that a large portion of
the interpretation hinge on this, it would be nice to understand the sensitivity here. (Ultimately I think this will not totally the
conclusions, as changes are readily visible anyways so I think that is still on safe ground no matter what).
Triviality - Your third harmonic has a typo and should be 265 nm not 263 nm assuming 795 nm fundamental.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Malvestuto and collaborators present a carbon 𝐾-edge RIXS pump-probe study of graphite. We
believe the authors are the first to have considered ultrafast RIXS measurements of phonons. We
consequently hold the methodological innovation and ambition of the work in very high regard.
That said, we have some scientific concerns.
1. The data in Figs. 2b and 2c appear to be cut off. The full shape of the elastic line on the right is
not visible, and the complete extent of the key inelastic component is also not shown. It is
difficult to determine which values correspond to zero intensity due to the same issue of cut-offs.
The full extent of the spectra should be plotted, if available. If these data were not collected, a
comment should be added to the text.
2. The energy resolution of the experiment (350 meV) is substantially larger than the energy scale
of the phonons (200 meV). As a result, the phonon series appears as a blob rather than a sequence
of peaks. Individual phonons cannot be identified in the data, and the first order phonon cannot be
unambiguously separated from the elastic line. We highlight this because it unfortunately limits
the information content and the degree of certainty with which conclusions can be drawn.
3. In equilibrium, it has been previously shown that the low-energy window is dominated by
phonons. In the transient state, however, carriers are excited and may be scattered within a low-
energy electronic continuum. How can the authors exclude a contribution from this effect?
4. The off-resonant spectra in Fig. 2b show significant structure, dropping to lower values around
–1.2 eV and then rising again. Given the plotting window, we cannot be sure whether this line
shape is indeed symmetric, as claimed in line 267.
5. We ask the authors to justify the procedure of scaling the off-resonant spectrum to match the
intensity at zero energy and then subtracting it. This does not necessarily seem like a robust
method for isolating the phonons, given (a) the intensity away from the inelastic region,
as mentioned above, and (b) the fact that some phonon intensity will appear at 0 eV due to the
energy resolution being larger than the phonon energy.
6. The Ament model has not been shown to effectively explain the overtone modes in graphite.
Previous studies have demonstrated that the data cannot be explained solely in terms of
overtones of the Γ-point phonon but instead involve combinations of phonons from different
parts of the Brillouin zone for higher-order overtones (see Refs. [1,2]). In light of this, it is unclear
whether Equation 1 is appropriate for the data. Furthermore, Equation 1 clearly yields a
prediction for the full shape of the spectrum as a function of energy and not just a prediction for
the total intensity. It is concerning not to see a comparison between the predicted energy
dependent intensity for the model and data in the draft. This must be added.
7. The value of 𝑀 from [1] has been contested in [2]. This controversy needs to be acknowledged
and discussed.
8. It would be valuable to include some discussion situating the present work in the context of
other XFEL RIXS experiments. Only a handful of ultrafast XFEL RIXS studies probing
quasiparticles have been published since the first experiments about a decade ago, so it should
be straightforward to provide a comprehensive overview.
Overall, this work is quite novel in many respects, and we are glad to see it carried out. However,
we have concerns regarding both the experiment and the data analysis. Conducting the
experiment with an energy resolution that cannot resolve the phonons in question poses a
serious limitation to the information obtained.
For instance, it raises concerns about whether the intensity of the first
phonon can be uniquely distinguished from the elastic line, and whether other inelastic signals,
such as charge scattering, might exist out of equilibrium and might be mixed up with the phonon
spectrum. The analysis appears to rely on an equation that has not been shown to accurately model
the material under investigation. The omission of a basic test to verify whether the equation
reproduces the energy-dependent shape of the equilibrium and transient spectra is a significant
shortcoming of the current draft.
We believe these issues are, in principle, fixable to make the work publishable. However, we
remain skeptical about whether these problems can be resolved convincingly enough to merit
publication in Nature Communications.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, the authors present a time-resolved RIXS study on graphite, using a UV (4 eV) pump pulse to generate
photoexcited carriers and investigate the effect of photo-induced screening on the coupling between phonons and the core-
hole exciton created by the XUV probe photon.
By tuning the incident photon energy across the carbon K-edge resonance, the authors probe how photo-induced screening
modifies both the elastic (coherent) and inelastic (incoherent) parts of the RIXS spectrum associated with the Jahn-Teller
(JT) distortion from exciton-phonon coupling. While individual phonon peaks are not fully resolved, the spectral changes are
consistent with prior literature.
Strengths:
• The experimental dataset is valuable and adds time-domain insight into exciton-phonon coupling and screening effects in
graphite.
• The use of time-resolved RIXS to study suppression of incoherent phonon-related spectral features is a promising
approach.
Major concerns:
1. Clarity of interpretation:
The manuscript’s discussion switches between “exciton-phonon coupling” and “electron-phonon coupling” when describing
the fits of parameter R and its time evolution. This inconsistency creates ambiguity about the physical mechanism driving the
observed spectral changes. It is crucial for the authors to clarify whether the spectral dynamics arise predominantly from
changes in the JT distortion due to exciton-phonon coupling, or from broader electron-phonon interactions affected by
screening.
2. Ambiguity in spectral origin:
The manuscript sometimes leaves unclear whether the changes in spectra with detuning or pump delay arise from
modifications to the JT distortion or from screening effects, making interpretation difficult for readers.
3. Novelty claims:
The authors state that this is among the first demonstrations of time-resolved RIXS. However, to my knowledge, multiple
recent reviews and studies have demonstrated tr-RIXS probing dynamical processes and phase transitions in various
materials. Additionally, electron-phonon coupling in graphite has been extensively studied previously. The present work’s
novelty lies primarily in demonstrating the time-domain suppression of incoherent exciton-phonon related features via
photoinduced screening, which is sometimes obscured in the manuscript’s framing. The authors should revise their novelty
claims accordingly.
4. Suitability for Nature Communications:
While the data are valuable, I am not currently convinced the manuscript meets the threshold for publication in Nature
Communications without addressing the above issues, especially clarity and novelty. Improvement in the discussion of
exciton vs electron phonon coupling and stronger justification of the unique insight provided by their experimental approach
would significantly enhance the manuscript.
________________________________________
General comments:
• Citation clarity could be improved. For example, line 136 cites six references on JT distortion, but the exact source of the
quoted JT magnitude (line 139) is not explicitly referenced, forcing readers to track through earlier citations.
________________________________________
Specific comments:
Introduction:
1. Line 72: The authors use the term “radiation-matter interactions.” This phrasing is unusual in the community, which
typically uses “light-matter interactions.” Do the authors intend to include non-photon radiation (e.g., alpha, beta particles)? If
not, “light” might be a clearer choice.
2. Line 88: Referring to photoexcited carriers as an “electron-hole plasma” is not accurate here, as plasma usually implies a
state of free charges at high density. Consider revising this wording.
________________________________________
Figure 1:
• Fig. 1c:
a. The authors claim an energy resolution of 350 meV. How was this determined? The off-resonance peak appears broader
than 350 meV, which raises questions about the actual resolution.
b. Line 167 states a source bandwidth of ~60 meV, which seems contradictory to the 350 meV resolution claim. Please
clarify this discrepancy.
c. The “on-resonance” asymmetric peak shows small oscillations that do not match phonon peaks in the high-resolution
reference [12]. Could the authors comment on their origin?
• Fig. 1d: The colored pulses/arrows lack explanation in the caption and seem randomly assigned. Adding clear labels and
descriptions would improve reader understanding.
• Line 197: The statement about “anomalous valence quasiparticle lifetimes” attributed to a phonon bottleneck and band
structure deserves further elaboration. What specifically is anomalous, and how does graphite’s band structure produce this
behavior?
________________________________________
Figure 2:
• The static and pumped RIXS spectra (on and off resonance) are well presented. The authors attribute the asymmetric on-
resonance lineshape to exciton-phonon coupling, which diminishes off resonance and upon pumping due to screening.
• Line 313: The phrase “diminishing impact of the photoexcitation as photon energy deviates from resonance” is ambiguous.
Does this mean the screening effect weakens, the sensitivity to exciton-phonon coupling reduces off resonance, or the
exciton is less effectively excited? Clarification is needed.
• The pump-probe delay time shown in Fig. 2d is not specified and should be clearly stated.
• The discussion inconsistently refers to changes in the incoherent spectral weight (R) as due to exciton-phonon coupling in
some places, but attributes it to electron-phonon coupling in the Eq. 1 discussion (line 343). This contradiction is confusing
and should be resolved. Additionally, while screening should reduce exciton binding energy and lifetime, the authors
assume an unchanged exciton lifetime in the nonequilibrium state (line 337), which appears inconsistent.
________________________________________
Figure 3:
• Line 432: The off-resonance dynamics are attributed to thermal modification of interplanar distances, supported only by the
timescale (330 fs). This explanation is insufficiently developed. Could other mechanisms (e.g., optical phonons) contribute?
The authors should expand or qualify this interpretation.
________________________________________
If the authors address the above points and clarify their interpretation and novelty claims, this manuscript would be
significantly improved.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewer #1:
We appreciate this constructive suggestion. In the revised version, we have split Figure
2 into two separate figures:
• Figure 2a–b now contains the XAS and unpumped/pumped RIXS spectra.
• Figure 2c–d has been moved to a new Figure 3, dedicated to the analysis of
integrated inelastic spectral weights (R) and scaling factors (r), along with the
comparison to theoretical fits. We have expanded the figure captions to provide a
clearer explanation and ensure that the panels can be understood independently from
the main text. We have also summarized key elements of Fig. S2 (now included in
the main text as part of revised Figure 3) for clarity.
• In addition, we include in Figure 3b a conceptual illustration of the scattering process
duration τ(Ω) as a function of detuning, which clarifies the physical origin of the
observed spectral changes.
These changes follow the Reviewer’s suggestion and aim to improve clarity by separating
experimental observations from interpretative elements. The figure captions have also
been revised to ensure that each panel is self-contained and easily understood without
cross-referencing the main text or supplementary material.
In terms of science, a large portion of the results is pinned on the fitting of equation 1, which has
3 free parameters (although, the justification for using this equation is well supported and
justified).
The changes between the ground and excited state are quite large, but it is completely opaque to
the reader how sensitive these fitting values are. Given that a large portion of the interpretation
hinge on this, it would be nice to understand the sensitivity here. (Ultimately I think this will not
totally the conclusions, as changes are readily visible anyways so I think that is still on safe
ground no matter what).
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this thoughtful comment and for highlighting the
importance of clarifying the fitting procedure used in our analysis.
Although Equation 1 involves multiple parameters, we emphasize that only one
parameter—the exciton-phonon coupling strength M (or equivalently, the dimensionless
coupling constant g)—is treated as a free parameter in the fitting. The phonon energy ω₀
= 0.196 eV and the core-hole lifetime broadening Γ = 0.304 eV are kept fixed throughout,
based on established values from the literature. Specifically, ω₀ corresponds to the energy
of the dominant E₂g phonon mode in graphite, and Γ reflects the intrinsic linewidth of the
carbon K-edge (Sette et al., 1990), using the relation Γ = γ/ω₀ with γ/ω₀ = 1.55. The
detuning energy W is an independently controlled experimental variable and not a fitting
parameter.
To address the Reviewer’s concern regarding the sensitivity and robustness of the
extracted coupling values, we have now included a detailed error and sensitivity analysis
in the revised Supplementary Information (Section A.6). This includes:
• A quantitative assessment of uncertainties in the fitted parameter g, incorporating
experimental noise and model fitting tolerance;
• A systematic test showing how moderate variations in the fixed input parameters
(Γ, Ω, and ω₀) influence the extracted values of g and the integrated spectral weight
R;
• A demonstration that, despite limited energy resolution, the observed reduction in
coupling strength g between unpumped and pumped conditions is robust and
statistically significant.
These results confirm that our main conclusions regarding photoinduced suppression of
exciton-phonon coupling remain valid within experimental uncertainties

We acknowledge the energy resolution (350 meV) is larger than the phonon energy (~200
meV), which precludes resolution of individual vibrational sidebands. However, previous
studies (e.g., Ref. 12 and Harada et al. [16]) demonstrate that in this resolution regime,
vibronic features manifest as asymmetric tails in the loss spectrum. Our interpretation is
based on the observed trends in the inelastic tail intensity across detuning and time delays.
These changes are consistent with modulation of vibronic coupling, rather than continuum
electronic states.
However, our analytical approach explicitly accounts for this resolution limitation by
focusing on the integrated inelastic spectral weight rather than the intensity of individual
phonon peaks. This methodology follows the strategy adopted in earlier RIXS studies at
the carbon K-edge with comparable or lower energy resolution with respect to our case,
including the work by Carlisle et al. and others, who interpreted the inelastic spectral
continuum as a cumulative effect of multiple phonon excitations.

Additionally, it is important to emphasize that the main goal of our study is not to extract
an absolute, high-precision value for the exciton-phonon coupling constant in
graphite, which is already well established in the literature. Instead, the focus is on
tracking the relative change in exciton-phonon coupling under non-equilibrium,
photoexcited conditions induced by the resonant π−π∗ optical pump. This relative change
is clearly observable, even with the available energy resolution.
Finally, this experiment demonstrates, using graphite as a model system, how the
extension of RIXS into the time domain can reveal dynamical changes in exciton-phonon

We have clarified this reasoning in the revised manuscript and have included an explicit
discussion in the Supplementary Information (Section A.8) to emphasize both the validity
and the limitations of our resolution-constrained approach.
3. In equilibrium, it has been previously shown that the low-energy window is dominated by
phonons. In the transient state, however, carriers are excited and may be scattered within a low-
energy electronic continuum. How can the authors exclude a contribution from this effect?
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important and nuanced point. In equilibrium, the
low-energy inelastic window of the carbon K-edge RIXS spectrum in graphite is indeed well
known to be dominated by phonon excitations.
In the transient state following photoexcitation, carriers are excited into the conduction
band, and in principle, they may scatter within an electronic continuum, potentially
contributing to a broad, featureless background at low energy loss. However, multiple
factors strongly argue against a significant contribution from this effect in our data:
Orbital symmetry selectivity of the RIXS process
The resonance condition used in this experiment corresponds to the excitation of a carbon
1s core electron into the unoccupied 2pσ* antibonding state. This sets the symmetry of the
intermediate state in the RIXS process. On the other hand, the optical pump excites
carriers predominantly from the π to π* bands at the M saddle point of the Brillouin zone,
which are states of 2pπ character. As noted by the Reviewer, after excitation, hot electrons
rapidly relax to lower-energy conduction states around the Dirac cone at the K point (panel
b of the attached figure). These relaxed states remain of 2pπ character and thus do not
overlap with the intermediate 2pσ* state probed in the RIXS process.
Consequently, the mismatch in orbital character and momentum between the conduction
band states populated by the pump and the intermediate state of the RIXS probe renders
the probability of electronic continuum scattering negligible. This is schematically illustrated
in the figure:
• Panel a: the optical pump excites electrons from the π valence band to π*
conduction band at the M point.
• Panel b: these hot electrons relax toward the Dirac cone at the K point via
electronic intraband processes, all within the π* manifold.
• Panel c: the probe photon promotes a core 1s electron to the 2pσ* state, forming
an intermediate exciton. The RIXS emission probes the relaxation of this state,
primarily through phonon-coupled de-excitation back to the ground state or low-
energy excitonic states.
Because the intermediate state of the RIXS process is defined by a transition into the 2pσ*
orbital and the pump-populated states lie within the 2pπ* manifold, there is no direct overlap
between the hot carrier population and the intermediate state. As a result, excess charge
in the conduction band does not contribute to the observed low-energy RIXS features.
Absence of broad spectral background in the experimental data:
In the pumped condition, the inelastic RIXS response retains a well-defined spectral
structure consistent with phonon excitations, despite the limited energy resolution (~350
meV). We do not observe the emergence of any broad or featureless background at low
energy loss that would indicate scattering from a low-energy electronic continuum. The
transient modifications are instead confined to the inelastic sideband region and remain
spectroscopically compatible with phonon-coupled RIXS emission. This is further
supported by our time- and energy-resolved analysis, which quantitatively reproduces the
observed spectral evolution using a phonon-based model..
Core-hole lifetime and selection rules suppress non-resonant channels:
The relatively short core-hole lifetime (Γ ~ 0.4 eV) and the strict resonance condition favor
inelastic channels involving well-defined excitonic intermediate states and symmetry-
allowed phonon couplings. Incoherent or off-resonant scattering channels—such as those
that might involve an electronic continuum—are strongly suppressed due to poor matrix
element overlap with the intermediate state.
4. The off-resonant spectra in Fig. 2b show significant structure, dropping to lower values around
–1.2 eV and then rising again. Given the plotting window, we cannot be sure whether this line
shape is indeed symmetric, as claimed in line 267.
Response: (see also response to comment 1) The energy range shown in Fig. 2b was
intentionally limited to the low-energy-loss region near zero energy loss, to focus on the
phonon-related inelastic response that is the central topic of this manuscript. This cropped
plotting window was chosen to avoid compressing the relevant low-energy features and to
improve the visibility of the phonon dynamics relative to the much more intense elastic line.
To clarify the full spectral context, we now provide in the Supplementary Information
(Supplementary Figure 2S, Section A.2) the complete measured off-resonance spectrum,
extending up to higher energy losses well into the valence band region (see also figure in
Response for issue number 1). As visible in this full-range plot, the observed drop in
intensity around –1.2 eV and the subsequent slight rise at higher energy loss do not
originate from any asymmetry of the elastic peak or from features related to the phonon
response. Instead, the intensity remains essentially constant (background counts) from 0
to approximately –5 eV and then begins to increase due to the onset of valence band
emission at larger energy losses (approximately –7 to –15 eV), where the core holes
created during the core absorption process are filled by electrons from the p-symmetry
projected valence band states of graphite.
This experimental observation confirms that the spectral rise at larger energy loss is
unrelated to the symmetry of the elastic or phonon features discussed in the manuscript.
For further clarity, we have added a note in the revised manuscript (see line 314), explicitly
stating that the energy window shown in Fig. 2b was cropped for clarity and that the
apparent spectral rise at larger energy loss is associated with the onset of valence band
emission.
A detailed study of the valence band emission and its pump-probe dynamics, which we
also measured at the carbon 2p resonance, will be the subject of a separate publication,
p
as it extends beyond the phonon-focused scope of the present work.
5. We ask the authors to justify the procedure of scaling the off-resonant spectrum to match the
intensity at zero energy and then subtracting it. This does not necessarily seem like a robust
method for isolating the phonons, given (a) the intensity away from the inelastic region,
as mentioned above, and (b) the fact that some phonon intensity will appear at 0 eV due to the
energy resolution being larger than the phonon energy.
Response:
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important methodological point. This comment
helped us to further clarify the rationale behind the off-resonance normalization and
subtraction procedure in the revised manuscript (see lines 319 ).
Our working assumption is that the elastic component of the RIXS spectrum serves as a
direct, proportional measure of the resonant X-ray absorption cross-section at each
incident photon energy. The elastic scattering intensity follows the absorption profile
because it results from direct scattering without energy loss, scaling with the number of
available core holes and the resonant enhancement. This assumption is supported by the
observed near-symmetric lineshape of the elastic peak, as shown by our off-resonance
spectrum.
Similarly, the inelastic scattering intensity from phonon overtones is also expected to scale
with the absorption cross-section, since the creation of multiple phonons is a second-order
resonant process driven by the same intermediate-state core hole population. Therefore,
by normalizing the off-resonant spectrum to match the elastic peak height at zero energy
loss, we ensure that both elastic and inelastic spectral weight are proportionally scaled
according to the cross-section at each excitation energy.
The goal of this normalization-subtraction procedure is to isolate the resonantly enhanced
inelastic spectral weight, removing the underlying energy-dependent absorption profile that
equally affects both elastic and inelastic contributions. This allows us to track the resonant
enhancement of the phonon-coupled RIXS signal as a function of detuning.
We are fully aware that the finite energy resolution causes some phonon-related intensity
to appear at 0 eV, leading to partial spectral overlap between elastic and phonon
components. However, the off-resonant reference spectrum already contains this
convolution of elastic and non-resonant contributions under the same instrumental
resolution. By using this reference and applying the same scaling to both elastic and
inelastic parts, we minimize potential systematic errors introduced by the resolution
broadening.
Importantly, the robustness of this approach is validated by the consistency between the
detuning-dependent inelastic intensity trends and the expected theoretical scaling from the
Ament model, as shown in Figure 3a.
6. The Ament model has not been shown to effectively explain the overtone modes in graphite.
Previous studies have demonstrated that the data cannot be explained solely in terms of overtones
of the Γ-point phonon but instead involve combinations of phonons from different parts of the
Brillouin zone for higher-order overtones (see Refs. [1,2]). In light of this, it is unclear whether
Equation 1 is appropriate for the data. Furthermore, Equation 1 clearly yields a prediction for the
full shape of the spectrum as a function of energy and not just a prediction for the total intensity. It
is concerning not to see a comparison between the predicted energy dependent intensity for the
model and data in the draft. This must be added.
Response:
We acknowledge that the Ament model simplifies the multi-phonon structure and does not
account for all phonon branches. However, within our resolution-limited regime, the loss
feature cannot resolve different contributions from phonon combinations. Equation 1
provides a tractable and physically motivated approximation for analyzing vibronic coupling
via a single mode. We have added a new panel (Figure R2) comparing the predicted
energy-dependent spectral shape from the model to our data. This comparison supports
the model’s relevance in our experiment.
We fully agree that the complete vibrational spectrum in graphite includes contributions
from phonons across different points of the Brillouin zone. In particular, prior high-
resolution studies (e.g., Feng et al., PRL 125, 116401 (2020); Dashwood et al., PRX 11,
041052 (2021)) have demonstrated that multiple phonon modes—including the zone-
center E₂g (G mode) and the zone-edge A₁′ (2D mode)—can contribute to the overtone
structure in static RIXS spectra.
However, those results were obtained under optimized conditions for energy resolution
and symmetry detection, with resolutions better than 100 meV. In contrast, our experiment
was performed in a pump-probe configuration at moderate energy resolution (~350 meV),
where the individual overtone peaks are spectrally unresolved. In this regime, the RIXS
spectral response is dominated by the zone-center E₂g phonon, which couples strongly at
the Γ point due to dipole selection rules associated with the C 1s → σ* resonance. This
resonance and momentum selectivity has been extensively discussed in the literature and
justifies the use of a single-mode, Γ-centered optical phonon model for interpreting our
spectra.
Scope and justification for the Ament model
Our use of the Ament formalism is guided by a clear and constrained purpose: to model
the total inelastic spectral weight (i.e., integrated intensity) as a function of detuning from
resonance (Δ), rather than to resolve individual phonon contributions. As the Reviewer
correctly notes, the full spectral shape in graphite at high order involves contributions
from phonons at various momenta and polarizations. Capturing these details requires a full
Green’s function treatment, as performed by Dashwood et al. (PRX 2021), which is beyond
the scope of the current work.
Instead, our analysis follows the approach of previous works (e.g., Carlisle et al., PRL 74,
1234 (1995); Feng et al., PRL 125, 116401 (2020); Rossi et al., PRL 123, 027001 (2019)),
where the Ament model is used in its integrated form to track the detuning dependence of
the inelastic weight. The model has proven successful in capturing qualitative trends in
resonant enhancement under moderate or limited resolution.
Clarification of equation and implementation
As clarified in the revised manuscript (lines 446-450) Equation 1 in our paper corresponds
to the full energy-dependent RIXS intensity derived from the single-site Ament model.
To directly address the Reviewer's request for a shape comparison, we now include in
the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Figure 3S and figure below) a detailed
figure with two panels:
• Panel A shows the measured on-resonance RIXS spectrum (smoothed, black line)
plotted together with the theoretical intensity envelope predicted by the Ament model
for Δ = –0.45 eV. We show both the convolved (red dashed line) and the unbroadened
stick-like (blue) spectra. The model captures the energy-dependent intensity
distribution reasonably well, particularly in terms of width and inelastic shoulder, within
the constraints of experimental resolution. A resolution-broadened elastic line (green
dashed-dot) is also included to show the elastic background shape.
• Panel B shows a full simulated RIXS intensity map I(ω, Δ), where the energy loss
axis (ω) is plotted against photon detuning (Δ). The map is calculated using the full Ament
model expression above and demonstrates how the total spectral envelope evolves
with detuning. The phonon resonance appears as a dispersive tail extending from the
elastic peak, showing increased intensity and broadening on resonance, consistent
with experimental observations.
While the Ament model does not reproduce the fine peak structure (which is unresolved in
our data) as demonstrated by Dashwood and others, these simulations demonstrate that
the overall envelope of the phonon sideband and its detuning-dependent modulation.
Summary:
• The Ament model is applied only to the total inelastic spectral weight and not to the
decomposition into individual phonon modes or overtones.
• The goal is not to reproduce the full overtone structure, but to quantify trends in the
integrated spectral weight due to resonant enhancement near the Γ-point E₂g phonon.
• This approach is experimentally justified by the limited resolution and the momentum
selectivity of the RIXS process at the C 1s → σ* edge.
• It is also consistent with prior studies (Feng et al., Rossi et al., Carlisle et al.) that used
integrated forms of the Ament model to describe similar systems under similar
constraints.
• Additional comparisons are now provided in Supplementary Figure 3S.
We believe these clarifications, together with the additional simulations and comparisons,
satisfactorily resolve the Reviewer’s concern.

Response: we thank the Reviewer for pointing out the controversy regarding the value of
the exciton-phonon coupling strength M reported in Ref. [1] (Feng et al., Phys. Rev. Lett.
up
125, 116401 (2020)) and contested in Ref. [2] (Dashwood et al., Phys. Rev. X 11, 041052
(2021)). We now explicitly acknowledge this issue in the revised manuscript (lines 510-
515).
In particular, Ref. [1] employed a phenomenological model assuming a single effective
phonon mode and extracted the coupling constants M and M based on fits to the RIXS
G A1’
intensity detuning curves. However, as highlighted in Ref. [2], this approach does not
account for the mixing of multiple phonon modes and their full momentum dependence,
which can significantly renormalize the spectral weight across the multiphonon excitations.
Dashwood et al. demonstrated, using a Green’s-function formalism that includes phonon
dispersion and intermediate-state mode mixing, that the multiphonon features in graphite’s
RIXS spectra can be more accurately described without invoking unrealistically large
values of the coupling constant.
While both studies agree on the qualitative observation that different phonon modes couple
differently to π* and σ* excitons, they differ on the quantitative magnitude of this coupling,
particularly for the G mode. This discrepancy underscores the importance of the underlying
theoretical framework: simplified models may lead to overestimated coupling constants if
the complex nature of the intermediate state is not fully captured.
In our manuscript, we maintain the use of detuning-dependent RIXS intensity as a means
to gauge exciton-phonon coupling, while acknowledging its limitations and the more
sophisticated treatment proposed in Ref. [2]. We now clarify that the reported coupling
constants should be interpreted as effective values within the approximations of our model,
and that further theoretical developments, such as those in Ref. [2], provide valuable
refinements for quantitatively accurate extraction of EPC parameters in graphite.
8. It would be valuable to include some discussion situating the present work in the context of
other XFEL RIXS experiments. Only a handful of ultrafast XFEL RIXS studies probing
quasiparticles have been published since the first experiments about a decade ago, so it should
be straightforward to provide a comprehensive overview.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. In the revised Introduction
and Discussion, we have now added references to prior tr-RIXS studies (e.g., Dean et al.,
Dantz et al., Mitrano et al.) and clarified that, while tr-RIXS has been demonstrated, our
work represents a first demonstration of time-domain suppression of vibronic features in a
van der Waals solid.
In response, we have added a dedicated paragraph to the end of the Introduction that
surveys the key developments in the field over the past decade. This new paragraph
(highlighted in red in the revised manuscript) reviews recent FEL-based tr-RIXS studies
that have probed transient electronic, magnetic, and orbital excitations in strongly
correlated materials such as cuprates, iridates, and vanadates. We then clearly delineate
the novelty of our work: to our knowledge, this is the first time-resolved RIXS experiment
resolving phonon-sideband dynamics at the carbon K-edge, and more specifically, the first observation
of the ultrafast modulation of exciton-phonon coupling due to photoinduced
screening in a light-element, weakly screened material such as graphite.
This distinction is now clearly articulated in the revised Introduction and Conclusions
(highlighted in red in the manuscript), where we situate our study in the context of the
limited number of tr-RIXS works that have targeted bosonic excitations. While phonon-
related features in graphite have been previously investigated in equilibrium using various
spectroscopies, our work goes further by probing how exciton-phonon interactions
evolve in the transient regime, in response to changes in electronic screening induced
by femtosecond optical excitation.
Importantly, the primary objective of our study is not to extract the static exciton-
phonon coupling constants, but to reveal how this coupling is dynamically modified
in time, shedding light on the interplay between charge carrier screening and vibronic
structure in a regime that is uniquely accessible through ultrafast core-level
spectroscopies.
We thank the Reviewer again for encouraging us to refine the framing of our contribution,
which we believe is now more precise and clearly contextualized within the state of the art.
Overall, this work is quite novel in many respects, and we are glad to see it carried out. However,
we have concerns regarding both the experiment and the data analysis. Conducting the
experiment with an energy resolution that cannot resolve the phonons in question poses a
serious limitation to the information obtained.
For instance, it raises concerns about whether the intensity of the first phonon can be uniquely
distinguished from the elastic line, and whether other inelastic signals, such as charge scattering,
might exist out of equilibrium and might be mixed up with the phonon spectrum. The analysis
appears to rely on an equation that has not been shown to accurately model the material under
investigation. The omission of a basic test to verify whether the equation reproduces the energy-
dependent shape of the equilibrium and transient spectra is a significant shortcoming of the
current draft.
We believe these issues are, in principle, fixable to make the work publishable. However, we
remain skeptical about whether these problems can be resolved convincingly enough to merit
publication in Nature Communications.
We once again are grateful for the constructive comments from Reviewer #2 and for
acknowledging that our work is quite novel in many respects. Also, we hope that we have
resolved all the issues raised by the Reviewer #2, and that the paper is now suitable for
