### Reviewer 2

Malvestuto and collaborators present a carbon 𝐾-edge RIXS pump-probe study of graphite. We
believe the authors are the first to have considered ultrafast RIXS measurements of phonons. We
consequently hold the methodological innovation and ambition of the work in very high regard.
That said, we have some scientific concerns.
1. The data in Figs. 2b and 2c appear to be cut off. The full shape of the elastic line on the right is
not visible, and the complete extent of the key inelastic component is also not shown. It is
difficult to determine which values correspond to zero intensity due to the same issue of cut-offs.
The full extent of the spectra should be plotted, if available. If these data were not collected, a
comment should be added to the text.
2. The energy resolution of the experiment (350 meV) is substantially larger than the energy scale
of the phonons (200 meV). As a result, the phonon series appears as a blob rather than a sequence
of peaks. Individual phonons cannot be identified in the data, and the first order phonon cannot be
unambiguously separated from the elastic line. We highlight this because it unfortunately limits
the information content and the degree of certainty with which conclusions can be drawn.
3. In equilibrium, it has been previously shown that the low-energy window is dominated by
phonons. In the transient state, however, carriers are excited and may be scattered within a low-
energy electronic continuum. How can the authors exclude a contribution from this effect?
4. The off-resonant spectra in Fig. 2b show significant structure, dropping to lower values around
–1.2 eV and then rising again. Given the plotting window, we cannot be sure whether this line
shape is indeed symmetric, as claimed in line 267.
5. We ask the authors to justify the procedure of scaling the off-resonant spectrum to match the
intensity at zero energy and then subtracting it. This does not necessarily seem like a robust
method for isolating the phonons, given (a) the intensity away from the inelastic region,
as mentioned above, and (b) the fact that some phonon intensity will appear at 0 eV due to the
energy resolution being larger than the phonon energy.
6. The Ament model has not been shown to effectively explain the overtone modes in graphite.
Previous studies have demonstrated that the data cannot be explained solely in terms of
overtones of the Γ-point phonon but instead involve combinations of phonons from different
parts of the Brillouin zone for higher-order overtones (see Refs. [1,2]). In light of this, it is unclear
whether Equation 1 is appropriate for the data. Furthermore, Equation 1 clearly yields a
prediction for the full shape of the spectrum as a function of energy and not just a prediction for
the total intensity. It is concerning not to see a comparison between the predicted energy
dependent intensity for the model and data in the draft. This must be added.
7. The value of 𝑀 from [1] has been contested in [2]. This controversy needs to be acknowledged
and discussed.
8. It would be valuable to include some discussion situating the present work in the context of
other XFEL RIXS experiments. Only a handful of ultrafast XFEL RIXS studies probing
quasiparticles have been published since the first experiments about a decade ago, so it should
be straightforward to provide a comprehensive overview.
Overall, this work is quite novel in many respects, and we are glad to see it carried out. However,
we have concerns regarding both the experiment and the data analysis. Conducting the
experiment with an energy resolution that cannot resolve the phonons in question poses a
serious limitation to the information obtained.
For instance, it raises concerns about whether the intensity of the first
phonon can be uniquely distinguished from the elastic line, and whether other inelastic signals,
such as charge scattering, might exist out of equilibrium and might be mixed up with the phonon
spectrum. The analysis appears to rely on an equation that has not been shown to accurately model
the material under investigation. The omission of a basic test to verify whether the equation
reproduces the energy-dependent shape of the equilibrium and transient spectra is a significant
shortcoming of the current draft.
We believe these issues are, in principle, fixable to make the work publishable. However, we
remain skeptical about whether these problems can be resolved convincingly enough to merit
publication in Nature Communications.

cumulative nature. In this formalism, the total inelastic weight, as described by the
summation over all overtone orders in Equation 1 of the manuscript, does not require
explicit spectral separation between the elastic line and the first phonon order. The
detuning dependence of the total inelastic spectral weight, even when unresolved into
individual phonon peaks, contains all the relevant information on the exciton-phonon
coupling strength.
Indeed, Rossi et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 027001 (2019)) and others used the intensity of
the first resolved phonon overtone to extract the “electron-phonon coupling” constant at
higher energy resolution, but the same underlying formalism (the Einstein oscillator model
and the Ament formulation) governs the dependence of either the first overtone intensity
or the cumulative inelastic weight on the detuning. As can be seen from direct
comparison of the Ament formula for single-order versus total intensity, both I (Δ) and
total

Additionally, it is important to emphasize that the main goal of our study is not to extract
an absolute, high-precision value for the exciton-phonon coupling constant in
graphite, which is already well established in the literature. Instead, the focus is on
tracking the relative change in exciton-phonon coupling under non-equilibrium,
photoexcited conditions induced by the resonant π−π∗ optical pump. This relative change
is clearly observable, even with the available energy resolution.
Finally, this experiment demonstrates, using graphite as a model system, how the
extension of RIXS into the time domain can reveal dynamical changes in exciton-phonon
coupling, an aspect that remains inaccessible to static measurements, even those
performed at higher spectral resolution.
We have clarified this reasoning in the revised manuscript and have included an explicit
discussion in the Supplementary Information (Section A.8) to emphasize both the validity
and the limitations of our resolution-constrained approach.
3. In equilibrium, it has been previously shown that the low-energy window is dominated by
phonons. In the transient state, however, carriers are excited and may be scattered within a low-
energy electronic continuum. How can the authors exclude a contribution from this effect?
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important and nuanced point. In equilibrium, the
low-energy inelastic window of the carbon K-edge RIXS spectrum in graphite is indeed well
known to be dominated by phonon excitations.
In the transient state following photoexcitation, carriers are excited into the conduction
band, and in principle, they may scatter within an electronic continuum, potentially
contributing to a broad, featureless background at low energy loss. However, multiple
factors strongly argue against a significant contribution from this effect in our data:
Orbital symmetry selectivity of the RIXS process
The resonance condition used in this experiment corresponds to the excitation of a carbon
1s core electron into the unoccupied 2pσ* antibonding state. This sets the symmetry of the
intermediate state in the RIXS process. On the other hand, the optical pump excites
carriers predominantly from the π to π* bands at the M saddle point of the Brillouin zone,
which are states of 2pπ character. As noted by the Reviewer, after excitation, hot electrons
rapidly relax to lower-energy conduction states around the Dirac cone at the K point (panel
b of the attached figure). These relaxed states remain of 2pπ character and thus do not
overlap with the intermediate 2pσ* state probed in the RIXS process.
Consequently, the mismatch in orbital character and momentum between the conduction
band states populated by the pump and the intermediate state of the RIXS probe renders
the probability of electronic continuum scattering negligible. This is schematically illustrated
in the figure:
• Panel a: the optical pump excites electrons from the π valence band to π*
conduction band at the M point.
• Panel b: these hot electrons relax toward the Dirac cone at the K point via
electronic intraband processes, all within the π* manifold.
• Panel c: the probe photon promotes a core 1s electron to the 2pσ* state, forming
an intermediate exciton. The RIXS emission probes the relaxation of this state,
primarily through phonon-coupled de-excitation back to the ground state or low-
energy excitonic states.
Because the intermediate state of the RIXS process is defined by a transition into the 2pσ*
orbital and the pump-populated states lie within the 2pπ* manifold, there is no direct overlap
between the hot carrier population and the intermediate state. As a result, excess charge
in the conduction band does not contribute to the observed low-energy RIXS features.
Absence of broad spectral background in the experimental data:
In the pumped condition, the inelastic RIXS response retains a well-defined spectral
structure consistent with phonon excitations, despite the limited energy resolution (~350
meV). We do not observe the emergence of any broad or featureless background at low
energy loss that would indicate scattering from a low-energy electronic continuum. The
transient modifications are instead confined to the inelastic sideband region and remain
spectroscopically compatible with phonon-coupled RIXS emission. This is further
supported by our time- and energy-resolved analysis, which quantitatively reproduces the
observed spectral evolution using a phonon-based model..
Core-hole lifetime and selection rules suppress non-resonant channels:
The relatively short core-hole lifetime (Γ ~ 0.4 eV) and the strict resonance condition favor
inelastic channels involving well-defined excitonic intermediate states and symmetry-
allowed phonon couplings. Incoherent or off-resonant scattering channels—such as those
that might involve an electronic continuum—are strongly suppressed due to poor matrix
element overlap with the intermediate state.
4. The off-resonant spectra in Fig. 2b show significant structure, dropping to lower values around
–1.2 eV and then rising again. Given the plotting window, we cannot be sure whether this line
shape is indeed symmetric, as claimed in line 267.
Response: (see also response to comment 1) The energy range shown in Fig. 2b was
intentionally limited to the low-energy-loss region near zero energy loss, to focus on the
phonon-related inelastic response that is the central topic of this manuscript. This cropped
plotting window was chosen to avoid compressing the relevant low-energy features and to
improve the visibility of the phonon dynamics relative to the much more intense elastic line.
To clarify the full spectral context, we now provide in the Supplementary Information
(Supplementary Figure 2S, Section A.2) the complete measured off-resonance spectrum,
extending up to higher energy losses well into the valence band region (see also figure in
Response for issue number 1). As visible in this full-range plot, the observed drop in
intensity around –1.2 eV and the subsequent slight rise at higher energy loss do not
originate from any asymmetry of the elastic peak or from features related to the phonon
response. Instead, the intensity remains essentially constant (background counts) from 0
to approximately –5 eV and then begins to increase due to the onset of valence band
emission at larger energy losses (approximately –7 to –15 eV), where the core holes
created during the core absorption process are filled by electrons from the p-symmetry
projected valence band states of graphite.
This experimental observation confirms that the spectral rise at larger energy loss is
unrelated to the symmetry of the elastic or phonon features discussed in the manuscript.
For further clarity, we have added a note in the revised manuscript (see line 314), explicitly
stating that the energy window shown in Fig. 2b was cropped for clarity and that the
apparent spectral rise at larger energy loss is associated with the onset of valence band
emission.
A detailed study of the valence band emission and its pump-probe dynamics, which we
also measured at the carbon 2p resonance, will be the subject of a separate publication,
p
as it extends beyond the phonon-focused scope of the present work.
5. We ask the authors to justify the procedure of scaling the off-resonant spectrum to match the
intensity at zero energy and then subtracting it. This does not necessarily seem like a robust
method for isolating the phonons, given (a) the intensity away from the inelastic region,
as mentioned above, and (b) the fact that some phonon intensity will appear at 0 eV due to the
energy resolution being larger than the phonon energy.
Response:
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important methodological point. This comment
helped us to further clarify the rationale behind the off-resonance normalization and
subtraction procedure in the revised manuscript (see lines 319 ).
Our working assumption is that the elastic component of the RIXS spectrum serves as a
direct, proportional measure of the resonant X-ray absorption cross-section at each
incident photon energy. The elastic scattering intensity follows the absorption profile
because it results from direct scattering without energy loss, scaling with the number of
available core holes and the resonant enhancement. This assumption is supported by the
observed near-symmetric lineshape of the elastic peak, as shown by our off-resonance
spectrum.
Similarly, the inelastic scattering intensity from phonon overtones is also expected to scale
with the absorption cross-section, since the creation of multiple phonons is a second-order
resonant process driven by the same intermediate-state core hole population. Therefore,
by normalizing the off-resonant spectrum to match the elastic peak height at zero energy
loss, we ensure that both elastic and inelastic spectral weight are proportionally scaled
according to the cross-section at each excitation energy.
The goal of this normalization-subtraction procedure is to isolate the resonantly enhanced
inelastic spectral weight, removing the underlying energy-dependent absorption profile that
equally affects both elastic and inelastic contributions. This allows us to track the resonant
enhancement of the phonon-coupled RIXS signal as a function of detuning.
We are fully aware that the finite energy resolution causes some phonon-related intensity
to appear at 0 eV, leading to partial spectral overlap between elastic and phonon
components. However, the off-resonant reference spectrum already contains this
convolution of elastic and non-resonant contributions under the same instrumental
resolution. By using this reference and applying the same scaling to both elastic and
inelastic parts, we minimize potential systematic errors introduced by the resolution
broadening.
Importantly, the robustness of this approach is validated by the consistency between the
detuning-dependent inelastic intensity trends and the expected theoretical scaling from the
Ament model, as shown in Figure 3a.
6. The Ament model has not been shown to effectively explain the overtone modes in graphite.
Previous studies have demonstrated that the data cannot be explained solely in terms of overtones
of the Γ-point phonon but instead involve combinations of phonons from different parts of the
Brillouin zone for higher-order overtones (see Refs. [1,2]). In light of this, it is unclear whether
Equation 1 is appropriate for the data. Furthermore, Equation 1 clearly yields a prediction for the
full shape of the spectrum as a function of energy and not just a prediction for the total intensity. It
is concerning not to see a comparison between the predicted energy dependent intensity for the
model and data in the draft. This must be added.
Response:
We acknowledge that the Ament model simplifies the multi-phonon structure and does not
account for all phonon branches. However, within our resolution-limited regime, the loss
feature cannot resolve different contributions from phonon combinations. Equation 1
provides a tractable and physically motivated approximation for analyzing vibronic coupling
via a single mode. We have added a new panel (Figure R2) comparing the predicted
energy-dependent spectral shape from the model to our data. This comparison supports
the model’s relevance in our experiment.
We fully agree that the complete vibrational spectrum in graphite includes contributions
from phonons across different points of the Brillouin zone. In particular, prior high-
resolution studies (e.g., Feng et al., PRL 125, 116401 (2020); Dashwood et al., PRX 11,
041052 (2021)) have demonstrated that multiple phonon modes—including the zone-
center E₂g (G mode) and the zone-edge A₁′ (2D mode)—can contribute to the overtone
structure in static RIXS spectra.
However, those results were obtained under optimized conditions for energy resolution
and symmetry detection, with resolutions better than 100 meV. In contrast, our experiment
was performed in a pump-probe configuration at moderate energy resolution (~350 meV),
where the individual overtone peaks are spectrally unresolved. In this regime, the RIXS
spectral response is dominated by the zone-center E₂g phonon, which couples strongly at
the Γ point due to dipole selection rules associated with the C 1s → σ* resonance. This
resonance and momentum selectivity has been extensively discussed in the literature and
justifies the use of a single-mode, Γ-centered optical phonon model for interpreting our
spectra.
Scope and justification for the Ament model
Our use of the Ament formalism is guided by a clear and constrained purpose: to model
the total inelastic spectral weight (i.e., integrated intensity) as a function of detuning from
resonance (Δ), rather than to resolve individual phonon contributions. As the Reviewer
correctly notes, the full spectral shape in graphite at high order involves contributions
from phonons at various momenta and polarizations. Capturing these details requires a full
Green’s function treatment, as performed by Dashwood et al. (PRX 2021), which is beyond
the scope of the current work.
Instead, our analysis follows the approach of previous works (e.g., Carlisle et al., PRL 74,
1234 (1995); Feng et al., PRL 125, 116401 (2020); Rossi et al., PRL 123, 027001 (2019)),
where the Ament model is used in its integrated form to track the detuning dependence of
the inelastic weight. The model has proven successful in capturing qualitative trends in
resonant enhancement under moderate or limited resolution.
Clarification of equation and implementation
As clarified in the revised manuscript (lines 446-450) Equation 1 in our paper corresponds
to the full energy-dependent RIXS intensity derived from the single-site Ament model.
To directly address the Reviewer's request for a shape comparison, we now include in
the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Figure 3S and figure below) a detailed
figure with two panels:
• Panel A shows the measured on-resonance RIXS spectrum (smoothed, black line)
plotted together with the theoretical intensity envelope predicted by the Ament model
for Δ = –0.45 eV. We show both the convolved (red dashed line) and the unbroadened
stick-like (blue) spectra. The model captures the energy-dependent intensity
distribution reasonably well, particularly in terms of width and inelastic shoulder, within
the constraints of experimental resolution. A resolution-broadened elastic line (green
dashed-dot) is also included to show the elastic background shape.
• Panel B shows a full simulated RIXS intensity map I(ω, Δ), where the energy loss
axis (ω) is plotted against photon detuning (Δ). The map is calculated using the full Ament
model expression above and demonstrates how the total spectral envelope evolves
with detuning. The phonon resonance appears as a dispersive tail extending from the
elastic peak, showing increased intensity and broadening on resonance, consistent
with experimental observations.
While the Ament model does not reproduce the fine peak structure (which is unresolved in
our data) as demonstrated by Dashwood and others, these simulations demonstrate that
the overall envelope of the phonon sideband and its detuning-dependent modulation.
Summary:
• The Ament model is applied only to the total inelastic spectral weight and not to the
decomposition into individual phonon modes or overtones.
• The goal is not to reproduce the full overtone structure, but to quantify trends in the
integrated spectral weight due to resonant enhancement near the Γ-point E₂g phonon.
• This approach is experimentally justified by the limited resolution and the momentum
selectivity of the RIXS process at the C 1s → σ* edge.
• It is also consistent with prior studies (Feng et al., Rossi et al., Carlisle et al.) that used
integrated forms of the Ament model to describe similar systems under similar
constraints.
• Additional comparisons are now provided in Supplementary Figure 3S.
We believe these clarifications, together with the additional simulations and comparisons,
satisfactorily resolve the Reviewer’s concern.

Response: we thank the Reviewer for pointing out the controversy regarding the value of
the exciton-phonon coupling strength M reported in Ref. [1] (Feng et al., Phys. Rev. Lett.
up
125, 116401 (2020)) and contested in Ref. [2] (Dashwood et al., Phys. Rev. X 11, 041052
(2021)). We now explicitly acknowledge this issue in the revised manuscript (lines 510-
515).
In particular, Ref. [1] employed a phenomenological model assuming a single effective
phonon mode and extracted the coupling constants M and M based on fits to the RIXS
G A1’
intensity detuning curves. However, as highlighted in Ref. [2], this approach does not
account for the mixing of multiple phonon modes and their full momentum dependence,
which can significantly renormalize the spectral weight across the multiphonon excitations.
Dashwood et al. demonstrated, using a Green’s-function formalism that includes phonon
dispersion and intermediate-state mode mixing, that the multiphonon features in graphite’s
RIXS spectra can be more accurately described without invoking unrealistically large
values of the coupling constant.
While both studies agree on the qualitative observation that different phonon modes couple
differently to π* and σ* excitons, they differ on the quantitative magnitude of this coupling,
particularly for the G mode. This discrepancy underscores the importance of the underlying
theoretical framework: simplified models may lead to overestimated coupling constants if
the complex nature of the intermediate state is not fully captured.
In our manuscript, we maintain the use of detuning-dependent RIXS intensity as a means
to gauge exciton-phonon coupling, while acknowledging its limitations and the more
sophisticated treatment proposed in Ref. [2]. We now clarify that the reported coupling
constants should be interpreted as effective values within the approximations of our model,
and that further theoretical developments, such as those in Ref. [2], provide valuable
refinements for quantitatively accurate extraction of EPC parameters in graphite.
8. It would be valuable to include some discussion situating the present work in the context of
other XFEL RIXS experiments. Only a handful of ultrafast XFEL RIXS studies probing
quasiparticles have been published since the first experiments about a decade ago, so it should
be straightforward to provide a comprehensive overview.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. In the revised Introduction
and Discussion, we have now added references to prior tr-RIXS studies (e.g., Dean et al.,
Dantz et al., Mitrano et al.) and clarified that, while tr-RIXS has been demonstrated, our
work represents a first demonstration of time-domain suppression of vibronic features in a
van der Waals solid.
In response, we have added a dedicated paragraph to the end of the Introduction that
surveys the key developments in the field over the past decade. This new paragraph
(highlighted in red in the revised manuscript) reviews recent FEL-based tr-RIXS studies
that have probed transient electronic, magnetic, and orbital excitations in strongly
correlated materials such as cuprates, iridates, and vanadates. We then clearly delineate
the novelty of our work: to our knowledge, this is the first time-resolved RIXS experiment
resolving phonon-sideband dynamics at the carbon K-edge, and more specifically, the first observation
of the ultrafast modulation of exciton-phonon coupling due to photoinduced
screening in a light-element, weakly screened material such as graphite.
This distinction is now clearly articulated in the revised Introduction and Conclusions
(highlighted in red in the manuscript), where we situate our study in the context of the
limited number of tr-RIXS works that have targeted bosonic excitations. While phonon-
related features in graphite have been previously investigated in equilibrium using various
spectroscopies, our work goes further by probing how exciton-phonon interactions
evolve in the transient regime, in response to changes in electronic screening induced
by femtosecond optical excitation.
Importantly, the primary objective of our study is not to extract the static exciton-
phonon coupling constants, but to reveal how this coupling is dynamically modified
in time, shedding light on the interplay between charge carrier screening and vibronic
structure in a regime that is uniquely accessible through ultrafast core-level
spectroscopies.
We thank the Reviewer again for encouraging us to refine the framing of our contribution,
which we believe is now more precise and clearly contextualized within the state of the art.
Overall, this work is quite novel in many respects, and we are glad to see it carried out. However,
we have concerns regarding both the experiment and the data analysis. Conducting the
experiment with an energy resolution that cannot resolve the phonons in question poses a
serious limitation to the information obtained.
For instance, it raises concerns about whether the intensity of the first phonon can be uniquely
distinguished from the elastic line, and whether other inelastic signals, such as charge scattering,
might exist out of equilibrium and might be mixed up with the phonon spectrum. The analysis
appears to rely on an equation that has not been shown to accurately model the material under
investigation. The omission of a basic test to verify whether the equation reproduces the energy-
dependent shape of the equilibrium and transient spectra is a significant shortcoming of the
current draft.
We believe these issues are, in principle, fixable to make the work publishable. However, we
remain skeptical about whether these problems can be resolved convincingly enough to merit
publication in Nature Communications.
We once again are grateful for the constructive comments from Reviewer #2 and for
acknowledging that our work is quite novel in many respects. Also, we hope that we have
resolved all the issues raised by the Reviewer #2, and that the paper is now suitable for

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors present a time-resolved RIXS study on graphite, using a UV (4
eV) pump pulse to generate photoexcited carriers and investigate the effect of photo-induced
screening on the coupling between phonons and the core-hole exciton created by the XUV probe
photon.
By tuning the incident photon energy across the carbon K-edge resonance, the authors probe
how photo-induced screening modifies both the elastic (coherent) and inelastic (incoherent) parts
of the RIXS spectrum associated with the Jahn-Teller (JT) distortion from exciton-phonon
coupling. While individual phonon peaks are not fully resolved, the spectral changes are
consistent with prior literature.
Strengths:
• The experimental dataset is valuable and adds time-domain insight into exciton-phonon
coupling and screening effects in graphite.
• The use of time-resolved RIXS to study suppression of incoherent phonon-related spectral
features is a promising approach.
Major concerns:
1. Clarity of interpretation:
The manuscript’s discussion switches between “exciton-phonon coupling” and “electron-phonon
coupling” when describing the fits of parameter R and its time evolution. This inconsistency
creates ambiguity about the physical mechanism driving the observed spectral changes. It is
crucial for the authors to clarify whether the spectral dynamics arise predominantly from changes
in the JT distortion due to exciton-phonon coupling, or from broader electron-phonon interactions
affected by screening.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this ambiguity. We have carefully revised the
manuscript to consistently use 'exciton-phonon coupling' when discussing the interaction
between the core-exciton and phonons, and reserve 'electron-phonon coupling' for general
valence band processes. The reduction in the incoherent loss signal is attributed to
transient screening that suppresses the Jahn-Teller distortion of the core-exciton complex.
This causal sequence is now more clearly stated in the revised Sections 3 and 4.
In our study, the parameter R reflects the intensity of the phonon sideband associated with
vibronic scattering at the carbon K edge under resonant conditions. This sideband arises
from the coupling between the core-exciton—formed by the strongly localized 1s core hole
and a photoexcited electron in the σ∗ conduction band—and zone-centre optical phonons,
primarily of E symmetry. Therefore, the relevant interaction driving the spectral changes
2g
in our experiment is exciton-phonon coupling, not generic electron-phonon coupling.
To avoid ambiguity, we have revised the manuscript throughout to consistently use the
term "exciton-phonon coupling" when referring to the physical mechanism underlying
the observed vibronic features.
The discussion of the Jahn-Teller distortion, which is mediated by the core-exciton,
further supports this assignment: the distortion originates from the symmetry-breaking
interaction between the core-exciton and lattice vibrations, as described in the literature
(e.g., \cite{Feng.2020}).
Moreover, the observed reduction in R under photoexcitation is interpreted as a decrease
in exciton-phonon coupling strength, resulting from enhanced screening of the core-hole
potential by the photoinjected electron-hole plasma. This screening weakens the
localization and binding energy of the exciton, thereby reducing its ability to distort the
lattice and generate multiple phonon excitations.
We have updated the relevant sections of the manuscript to reflect this clarification and
have included a dedicated note in the Supplementary Information outlining the excitonic
origin of the fitted spectral features.
2. Ambiguity in spectral origin: the manuscript sometimes leaves unclear whether the changes in
spectra with detuning or pump delay arise from modifications to the JT distortion or from
screening effects, making interpretation difficult for readers.
Response (see also the discussion at point 1):
we appreciate the Reviewer’s careful reading and fully acknowledge the need to clarify the
spectral origin of the changes observed with detuning and pump delay.
The concern regarding the distinction between effects driven by Jahn-Teller (JT) distortion
and those resulting from screening is well taken.
In our study, changes in the inelastic spectral weight and its temporal evolution are
interpreted primarily in terms of screening of the core-exciton by the photoinduced hot
electron distribution. This enhanced screening reduces the exciton binding energy,
weakens its spatial localisation, and consequently diminishes the strength of exciton-
phonon coupling responsible for the vibronic sidebands.
The reduction in vibronic intensity (quantified by the parameter R is thus an indirect
signature of screening and not a direct probe of JT distortion dynamics per se.
However, it is important to note that the JT distortion is mediated by exciton-phonon
coupling. Therefore, the suppression of the JT-induced lattice distortion under
photoexcitation is a consequence of the reduced exciton-phonon coupling strength. The
two effects—screening and JT suppression—are not independent, but causally linked:
screening weakens the exciton, which in turn reduces its ability to distort the lattice
via the JT mechanism.
To address the Reviewer’s concern and improve clarity, we have:
• Revised the relevant sections in the manuscript to explicitly trace the causal chain:
photoexcitation → enhanced screening → weakened exciton → reduced JT
distortion and phonon coupling.
• Added clarifying remarks in the Discussion section and in the caption of Figure 3
to make the physical interpretation transparent.
• Included a schematic summary in the Supplementary Information to illustrate how
detuning and pump delay affect the excitonic state and its coupling to phonons
through screening. Must be included.
We hope these revisions make the interpretation of the spectral changes clearer to the
reader and resolve the ambiguity highlighted by the Reviewer.
Ambiguity in spectral origin
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important point regarding the interpretation of the
spectral changes. We agree that distinguishing between the effects of Jahn-Teller (JT)
distortion and screening is crucial for a clear understanding of the data.
In our experiment, the multi-phonon spectral structure observed in the RIXS spectra
originates from the Jahn-Teller distortion associated with strong exciton-phonon
coupling in the core-excited state. This structure is well established in the literature and
reflects the displacement of the excited carbon atom from its equilibrium position due to
coupling with optical phonons.
The pump-induced changes to this structure—namely the suppression of the phonon
sidebands—are primarily attributed to modifications in the electronic screening
environment caused by the photoinduced electron-hole plasma. This screening reduces
the strength of the exciton-phonon coupling, effectively weakening the JT distortion and
altering the potential energy surface experienced by the core exciton.
Regarding detuning, it plays a complementary role: when the photon energy moves away
from resonance, the intermediate state becomes less excitonic and more delocalised,
reducing the strength and visibility of the phonon-coupled features. This energy-dependent
effect also modulates the apparent JT distortion, though in a static (non-dynamical)
fashion.
To clarify:
1. The origin of the phonon progression is the JT distortion due to exciton-phonon
coupling.
2. The modulation of this structure upon pumping reflects screening-induced
suppression of the exciton-phonon interaction.
3. The detuning dependence reflects the resonance condition of the RIXS
intermediate state and how effectively it couples to phonons.
We have revised the relevant sections of the manuscript to clarify these distinctions and
improve the interpretative framework for the reader.
3. Novelty claims:
The authors state that this is among the first demonstrations of time-resolved RIXS. However, to
my knowledge, multiple recent reviews and studies have demonstrated tr-RIXS probing
dynamical processes and phase transitions in various materials. Additionally, electron-phonon
coupling in graphite has been extensively studied previously. The present work’s novelty lies
primarily in demonstrating the time-domain suppression of incoherent exciton-phonon related
features via photoinduced screening, which is sometimes obscured in the manuscript’s framing.
The authors should revise their novelty claims accordingly.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s observation. In the revised manuscript, we clarify
that while tr-RIXS has been previously demonstrated, the novelty of our work lies in its
specific application to time-domain suppression of vibronic sidebands in graphite, a regime
not previously studied.
We fully acknowledge that in the past decade, a number of impactful time-resolved RIXS
(tr-RIXS) studies have successfully addressed ultrafast dynamics of spin, charge, and
orbital excitations—particularly in strongly correlated transition-metal systems such as
cuprates, iridates, and vanadates. These contributions have laid the groundwork for
expanding tr-RIXS into a broadly applicable tool in condensed matter physics.
In response to the Reviewer’s observation, we have carefully revised the manuscript to
clarify the novelty and scope of our work, avoiding any implication that our contribution
represents the first use of tr-RIXS as a general technique. Instead, we now state explicitly
that our study presents the first time-resolved RIXS experiment resolving phonon-
sideband dynamics at the carbon K-edge, and more specifically, the first observation
of the ultrafast modulation of exciton-phonon coupling due to photoinduced
screening in a light-element, weakly screened material such as graphite.
This distinction is now clearly articulated in the revised Introduction and Conclusions
(highlighted in red in the manuscript), where we situate our study in the context of the
limited number of tr-RIXS works that have targeted bosonic excitations. While phonon-
related features in graphite have been previously investigated in equilibrium using various
spectroscopies, our work goes further by probing how exciton-phonon interactions
evolve in the transient regime, in response to changes in electronic screening induced
by femtosecond optical excitation.
Importantly, the primary objective of our study is not to extract the static exciton-
phonon coupling constants, but to reveal how this coupling is dynamically modified
in time, shedding light on the interplay between charge carrier screening and vibronic
structure in a regime that is uniquely accessible through ultrafast core-level
spectroscopies.
We thank the Reviewer again for encouraging us to refine the framing of our contribution,
which we believe is now more precise and clearly contextualized within the state of the art.
4. Suitability for Nature Communications:
While the data are valuable, I am not currently convinced the manuscript meets the threshold for
publication in Nature Communications without addressing the above issues, especially clarity
and novelty. Improvement in the discussion of exciton vs electron phonon coupling and stronger
justification of the unique insight provided by their experimental approach would significantly
enhance the manuscript.

Fig. 1c:
a. The authors claim an energy resolution of 350 meV. How was this determined? The off-
resonance peak appears broader than 350 meV, which raises questions about the actual

Response to Reviewer Comment a:
We thank the Reviewer for pointing out the need to clarify how the energy resolution was
determined. The nominal energy resolution of ~350 meV was measured independently
using the elastic peak from diffuse scattering of the FEL beam off a silicon crystal
surface, as shown in the figure now attached to this rebuttal letter (Figure 1S in the
Supplementary Materials).
This calibration was performed off-resonance, far from any absorption edge, to avoid
distortions due to self-absorption, core-hole lifetime effects, or other resonant phenomena.
Moreover, the use of a clean, crystalline silicon surface, as opposed to the peeled graphite
sample, ensures minimal surface roughness and extrinsic broadening, which is essential
for an accurate determination of the resolution. The graph in figure R3 presents a
comparison between the spectral distribution of the FEL pulse as recorded by the online
TARDI spectrometer (blue curve, vertically offset and shown in a narrow energy window)
and the corresponding spectrum measured via diffuse scattering on a silicon surface using
the XES355 spectrometer (green and red curves). The red dashed line illustrates the ideal
energy response of the XES355, while the green curve represents the actual measured
lineshape, which includes the instrument's energy resolution and intrinsic count statistics.
We would also like to clarify that the spectra shown in the manuscript were subject to mild
smoothing to improve the visibility the spectral features (see figure R4, where dotted
curves represent raw data, continuous lines the smoothed spectra ). This smoothing
inevitably leads to some broadening of the elastic line, but it is applied uniformly across all
data and does not reflect the actual instrumental resolution. Therefore, the energy
resolution was not determined from the data shown in the main manuscript figures.
To further support this clarification, we include in the figure attached below both raw and
smoothed graphite spectra (the same data already included in Figure 2 in the
manuscript), acquired on-resonance and off-resonance. This comparison clearly shows
that the smoothing does affect the width of the elastic peak but does so consistently across
the dataset. The raw off-resonance elastic peak, measured on the silicon surface, is the
reference used for determining the experimental resolution of 350 meV.
We have added a brief description of the resolution calibration procedure in the
Supplementary Material (A1).

b. Line 167 states a source bandwidth of ~60 meV, which seems contradictory to the 350 meV

Response: we thank the reviewer for pointing out this apparent discrepancy. The 60 meV
bandwidth mentioned in line 167 refers to the intrinsic spectral width of the FEL pulse,
which is a property of the source. This value is consistent with the Fourier-limited
bandwidth of the seeded FERMI pulses and is measured for each single pulse using the
TARDI online spectrometer [Malvestuto et al., Rev. Sci. Instr. ].
However, the energy resolution of the experiment is determined not only by the source
bandwidth but also by the instrumental resolution of the XES355 spectrometer, which
broadens the detected features. In our case, the XES355 was characterized using diffuse
scattering from a silicon surface, yielding a total observed FWHM of 350 meV for the elastic
line. After deconvolving the independently measured FEL bandwidth (∼63 meV), the
intrinsic resolution of the XES355 spectrometer is estimated to be ∼344 meV. This value
reflects the actual resolving power of the spectrometer under the experimental geometry.
To clarify this, we now explicitly distinguish between the source bandwidth (∼60 meV) and
the spectrometer-limited experimental resolution (∼350 meV) in the revised text. A detailed
comparison between the TARDI and XES355 measurements is shown in the
Supplementary Information.
c. The “on-resonance” asymmetric peak shows small oscillations that do not match phonon
peaks in the high-resolution reference [12]. Could the authors comment on their origin?
Response: we thank the reviewer for this observation. The small oscillations visible on the
"on-resonance" asymmetric peak are not related to real phonon excitations. Instead, they

become more apparent after applying smoothing procedures, which we used to improve
visualization of broad spectral features. The oscillations have no physical significance and
are not reproducible across independent measurements.

Response
We thank the Reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity regarding the color-coded arrows in
Figure 1d. We agree that the absence of explicit labels and descriptions in the original
caption may hinder the reader’s understanding of the excitation and scattering processes
depicted.
To address this, we have thoroughly revised the caption for Figure 1d to explicitly

• The green solid arrow represents the optical pump excitation, resonantly
driving the π→π∗ transition at the M saddle point of the Brillouin zone.
• The blue dashed arrow depicts the X-ray probe excitation, corresponding to
the transition of a 1s core electron into the unoccupied σ∗ conduction band states
at the Γ point.
These revisions ensure that the schematic is now fully self-contained and interpretable

• Line 197: The statement about “anomalous valence quasiparticle lifetimes” attributed to a
phonon bottleneck and band structure deserves further elaboration. What specifically is
anomalous, and how does graphite’s band structure produce this behavior?
Response: the term “anomalous” refers to the observation that valence quasiparticles in
graphite can exhibit unusually long lifetimes in specific regions of the Brillouin zone,
particularly near the M point, in contrast to the short lifetimes typically expected due to
rapid electron-electron and electron-phonon scattering.
This behaviour arises from a phonon bottleneck effect, which is strongly influenced by
the peculiar topology of graphite’s electronic band structure. Specifically, at energies
below ~1.5 eV, the joint density of states for electron-hole pair creation at large momentum
transfer is suppressed, owing to the semimetallic nature and the Dirac-like dispersion near
the K and H points. In such a regime, decay pathways requiring large momentum transfer
(i.e., involving high-qq phonons or interband transitions) are energetically or kinematically
unfavourable.
Furthermore, the long screening length in graphite favours small-q (i.e., low-momentum)
electron-electron and electron-phonon scattering. However, for quasiparticles near saddle
points (such as the M point), decay via small-qq scattering is inefficient because the
available phase space for low-energy excitations at small momentum is limited. As a result,
these quasiparticles lack efficient relaxation channels, leading to longer lifetimes than
would be expected in more typical metallic or semiconducting systems.
This effect has been documented in both experimental and theoretical studies (e.g., Refs.
[Xu 1996, Breusing 2011, Spataru 2001, Piscanec 2004]), and represents a deviation from
the usual expectation that quasiparticle lifetimes decrease monotonically with energy due
to increased scattering phase space. We have now expanded the discussion in the
manuscript accordingly to clarify this point. (lines 211-220)
Figure 2:
The static and pumped RIXS spectra (on and off resonance) are well presented. The authors
attribute the asymmetric on-resonance lineshape to exciton-phonon coupling, which diminishes
off resonance and upon pumping due to screening.
Line 313: The phrase “diminishing impact of the photoexcitation as photon energy deviates from
resonance” is ambiguous. Does this mean the screening effect weakens, the sensitivity to
exciton-phonon coupling reduces off resonance, or the exciton is less effectively excited?
Clarification is needed.
Response: we acknowledge that the wording was ambiguous and have revised the text
to accurately reflect the intended meaning.
In this context, “photoexcitation” refers to the optical pump pulse that generates a non-
equilibrium charge distribution in the valence and conduction bands.
The core-resonant probe pulse used in the RIXS process is tuned across the XAS
resonance, and its detuning (Ω) determines the effective RIXS scattering time and the
strength of the core-exciton response.
As the probe photon energy is tuned away from the resonance, the system becomes
less sensitive to exciton-phonon coupling for two reasons:
1. The core-exciton is less efficiently formed off-resonance, and the process
becomes dominated by more delocalised particle-hole excitations with weaker
coupling to phonons.
2. The shorter effective RIXS scattering time at larger detuning reduces the
probability of observing scattering processes involving slower lattice dynamics,
such as phonon emission.
Therefore, although the optical pump remains unchanged, its effect becomes less visible
in the RIXS spectrum because the probe is no longer sampling a regime in which the
core-exciton–phonon interaction is strong or spectroscopically accessible.
We have revised the sentence in the manuscript accordingly, from line 380.

we thank the Reviewer for this helpful observation. In the revised manuscript, we have
clarified this point. The panel previously referred to as Figure 2d now appears as panel a

The discussion inconsistently refers to changes in the incoherent spectral weight (R) as due to
exciton-phonon coupling in some places, but attributes it to electron-phonon coupling in the Eq. 1
discussion (line 343). This contradiction is confusing and should be resolved. Additionally, while
screening should reduce exciton binding energy and lifetime, the authors assume an unchanged
exciton lifetime in the nonequilibrium state (line 337), which appears inconsistent.
Response:
We thank the Reviewer for carefully pointing out two important issues:
1. The inconsistent terminology in our manuscript regarding “exciton–phonon” versus
“electron–phonon” coupling, particularly in relation to the spectral weight changes
described by parameter R;
2. The assumption of an unchanged exciton lifetime in the nonequilibrium state, despite
the expectation that photoinduced screening could reduce the exciton binding energy
and hence its lifetime.
We address both concerns below and describe the revisions made to the manuscript to
improve clarity and consistency.
1. Exciton–Phonon vs Electron–Phonon Coupling
We agree with the Reviewer that the terminology must be used precisely. The parameter
R represents the intensity of the inelastic phonon sideband in the RIXS spectrum, which
arises from coupling between the core-exciton and lattice vibrations. The appropriate
physical mechanism governing this process is therefore exciton–phonon coupling,
rather than generic electron–phonon coupling.
We acknowledge that the use of “electron–phonon coupling” in the context of Equation 1
(in the previous manuscript version, line 343) was imprecise and potentially misleading.
Equation 1 is derived from the single-site model introduced by Ament et al., where the
lattice couples to the local charge density of the core-excited intermediate state.
Accordingly, the coupling is more accurately described as exciton–phonon in nature.
We have now revised the manuscript to use “exciton–phonon coupling” consistently in all
relevant discussions.
We note that while this distinction is now gaining traction in the literature, past RIXS studies
have often referred to the extracted coupling constants in terms of electron–phonon
coupling, especially in the context of superconductivity or many-body renormalisation
effects. However, as emphasized in a recent review by Gilmore et al. (Phys. Chem. Chem.
Phys., 2022), “the coupling constant extracted from a RIXS measurement is better viewed
as exciton–phonon coupling than the usual electron–phonon coupling initially sought.” This
reflects a growing consensus in the field, particularly when interpreting RIXS spectra under
strong resonance conditions, such as those involving core-excitons with well-defined
symmetries.
We hope this clarification resolves the apparent inconsistency and improves the
conceptual clarity for the reader.
2. Assumption of fixed exciton lifetime in the pumped state
The Reviewer also raises an important point about the assumption of a constant exciton
lifetime in the photoexcited state. While screening by the hot electrons may reduce the
binding energy of the core-exciton, it is important to distinguish between the exciton
binding energy and the core-hole decay lifetime.
In our analysis, the effective lifetime used in the fitting model refers to the core-hole
lifetime (represented by the parameter Γ), which is dominated by atomic Auger decay and
radiative recombination processes involving the deeply bound 1s core orbital. These
processes are largely unaffected by photoinduced changes in the valence carrier
population, particularly at the moderate excitation fluences used in this experiment.
Therefore, we have kept Γ fixed in both pumped and unpumped conditions, in order to
isolate and interpret changes in the exciton–phonon coupling strength, represented by
the parameter M in our model. A more comprehensive treatment including lifetime
broadening effects would require higher-resolution data and a multi-parameter global fit,
which goes beyond the scope of the present study.
To address this point, we have added a clarification in both the manuscript and
Supplementary Information.
Summary of Revisions in the Manuscript
• All references to “electron–phonon coupling” in the context of Equation 1 and the fitting
of R have been replaced with “exciton–phonon coupling” for consistency.
• An explicit statement has been added explaining why Γ is held constant in the fits, and
why this is a reasonable assumption given the nature of the core-excited state and the
spectral resolution of our data.
• A clarifying citation to Gilmore et al. (PCCP 2022) has been included to support our
interpretation of RIXS as a probe of exciton–phonon coupling.
We thank the Reviewer again for raising these important issues, which have helped us
improve the precision and clarity of the manuscript.
Figure 3:
Line 432: The off-resonance dynamics are attributed to thermal modification of interplanar
distances, supported only by the timescale (330 fs). This explanation is insufficiently developed.
Could other mechanisms (e.g., optical phonons) contribute? The authors should expand or
qualify this interpretation.
Response: we thank the Reviewer for this insightful observation. We agree that the
interpretation of the off-resonance dynamics as arising solely from thermal modification of
interplanar distances, based primarily on the observed 330 fs timescale, was insufficiently
developed in the original manuscript. We now clarify and expand this interpretation, as
requested.
In the off-resonance regime (i.e., for large detuning Ω≳ 1 eV), the effective RIXS scattering
time is below ~2 fs, which is too short for the system to probe slower lattice distortions such
as those associated with vibronic coupling or Jahn-Teller effects. The absence of overtone
sidebands and the full overlap of pumped and unpumped spectra in this regime confirm
that excitonic contributions are no longer spectroscopically accessible.
The observed dynamics at long delays (with a characteristic timescale of ~330 fs) are
instead attributed to thermal effects—specifically, the adiabatic response of the lattice to
energy transfer from the photoexcited electron-hole plasma to the phononic subsystem.
This assignment is consistent with time-resolved diffraction studies on graphite and related
materials, which report similar sub-picosecond timescales for the onset of lattice expansion
and contraction processes following ultrafast optical excitation (see e.g., Harb et al. 2011,
Carbone et al. 2008).
However, we agree that additional phonon-related mechanisms may contribute to
the observed dynamics. In particular, the rapid population of strongly coupled optical
phonons (SCOPs), which occurs on sub-100 fs timescales, could influence the transient
spectral weight through anharmonic coupling to acoustic modes or thermal expansion
effects. These SCOPs are known to dominate energy relaxation pathways in graphite
within the first picosecond (Kampfrath et al. 2005, Caruso et al. 2020).
To reflect this broader perspective, we have revised the manuscript text (line: 606).
We hope this expanded interpretation addresses the Reviewer’s concern and provides a
more complete picture of the dynamics observed in the off-resonant regime.
If the authors address the above points and clarify their interpretation and novelty claims, this
manuscript would be significantly improved.
